The equilibrium state can be understood through an equivalent process in which neutral and infected individuals draw each other out of a pool, resulting in an exact solution. The solution reveals how the number of connections, the duration over which connections are maintained, and the duration over which connections are randomly altered influence the equilibrium state. In particular, the model exhibits a critical point at which a small change in connection duration or alteration interval causes a significant increase in widespread infection. The model also exhibits hysteresis in cases where the equilibrium state is entered from different initial conditions. The model is supported by numerical simulations and is applicable to a wide range of power-law distributions.

This study examines a specific type of solution, the steady Cotton soliton, within the framework of 3-dimensional manifolds that have been equipped with Reeb vector fields and orthogonal potential vector fields. We demonstrate that this solution corresponds to a flat, oblique $\alpha$-Riemannian surface geometry.

A Python library called `irene` is being utilized to determine the parametric variables for the H1PDF, which is based on the fit framework developed by the H1 Collaboration. The `irene` library is employed to modify the H1PDF fit procedure, specifically to assess the behavior of parton distribution functions at different scales through the DGLAP evolution. To validate the `irene` library, a series of tests have been conducted to ensure accuracy. Furthermore, the `irene` library has been successfully used to fit the H1PDF data.

Previous studies have demonstrated that experience replay (ER) can significantly enhance policy gradient estimation in reinforcement learning through several variance reduction techniques. Notably, ER advances a batch of gradient estimates towards a target policy, with the understanding that the optimal method would achieve this goal efficiently. Building upon this, we propose a VRER framework that incorporates multiple ER algorithms, including distributional and structural-based methods. The framework showcases the computational benefits of these variance reduction techniques, with results indicating a notable enhancement of policy gradient estimation precision through the minimization of a task-agnostic policy loss. The VRER code is available at https://github.com/chenyiyong/VRER.

Libcommute is a versatile C library for computing molecular levels resulting from the interaction of two identical particles, with multiple level and model options available. To broaden its usefulness, we have created Python 3 bindings called pycommute, which provides an easy-to-use and intuitive interface to the libcommute functions. By doing so, we have also addressed several limitations of the original library, including the absence of level diagrams and graphical tools. Moreover, pycommute now includes various utility tools, such as file management and data visualization capabilities, making it an even more effective and user-friendly library for computing molecular levels.

Our research utilizes scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to examine the superconducting properties of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ films, particularly the superconducting gap around the zone corner, which has been underinferred previously due to experimental limitations. By optimizing the growth of these films and employing a 2D mapping technique, we resolved the gap anisotropy and distribution for several doses of Sr doping. The results show that the gap size at the zone corner is relatively constant at approximately 2.5$k_B T_c$, in contrast to the larger variation observed along the zone edge. The distribution of the gap size is nonuniform and varies nonmonotonically with Sr doping, exhibiting a more complex dependence than the zero-resistance critical temperature. The observed variation in the gap distribution is attributed to the competition between two types of order parameters, as predicted by theoretical models of iron-based superconductors. The findings of this study provide a more nuanced understanding of the superconducting properties of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ films and offer a basis for further investigation into the mechanisms governing the gap distribution in these materials.

We've recently introduced a generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and demonstrated its equivalence to the superbosonization formula using the bosonization technique, by transforming a specific class of deformed supersymmetric free field models into their corresponding Hubbard-Stratonovich forms. Taking the specific case where the deformed supersymmetric free field models comprise the generalized BCS superfluidity transition critical behavior, we find that applying the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation yields the 2D Kosterlitz-Nishiguchi critical behavior.

An analysis of the spin asymmetry of top quarks produced in pairs at an energy of 1.96 TeV is presented, using data collected by the CDF experiment at the Tevatron for an integrated luminosity of 9.6 inverse femtobarns. The value measured for the asymmetry is 0.031, which is in line with the predictions of the standard model and does not indicate any presence of physics beyond it.

We investigate how the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ layers influences the temperature dependence of the electronic relaxation time in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices through time-domain reflectometry. Contrary to expectations, thicker LaNiO$_3$ layers result in a more pronounced temperature dependence of the fast-relaxing component, which appears to be unaffected by changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness below 3 units. This behavior suggests a critical role for LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness in the carrier density of these superlattices, with potential implications for device performance.

Conversational AI systems must not only comprehend language but also develop mind
awareness, or theory of mind, to ensure effectiveness in dialog generation tasks.
Several methods exist for assessing theory of mind, but they don't consider the
social context essential for a conversational AI system working with humans.
Moreover, these assessment methods are often time-consuming and don't account
for the diversity of human thought. To address these limitations, we introduce a
new, more inclusive method for measuring the theory of mind of these systems,
called the Diverse Context Theory of Mind Assessment. This assessment tool
involves presenting the system with diverse social context scenarios in order to
determine its ability to understand the perspective of humans. We applied this
assessment tool to evaluate the theory of mind of both a machine learning-based
conversational AI system and a human user, and found that the system excels in
generating responses, but struggles with content, whereas humans exhibit the
opposite tendency. Notably, our results show that the diversity of context has
a significant impact on the system's performance, outperforming traditional
assessment methods.

Researchers analyzing the performance of future 6G wireless communication systems will likely need to study the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and changing phase shifts of reflecting coefficients on future wideband wireless communication systems. Due to increased bandwidth and the increased number of reflecting surfaces, future systems will experience more pronounced spatial correlations. A new dual-scattering model is introduced, which shows that the reflection coefficients' phase shifts are no longer independent and identically distributed. The model also highlights the challenge of measuring the distributions of fading and phase shifts directly. Instead, the distributions can only be characterized through their second-moment properties. A new approach is introduced to derive the capacity of wideband wireless communication systems by analyzing the distributions of their sum through the use of its second-moment properties. The results show that the distributions of capacity are skewed and heavily influenced by the correlations of fading and phase shifts. The model is then used to study the impact of different parameters on the capacity of future wireless communication systems. The results show that the capacity of future systems will be heavily influenced by the correlations of fading and phase shifts. The study also highlights the limitations of previous models in analyzing the capacity of future systems. The results also show that the capacity of future systems will be heavily influenced by the bandwidth used. The study also highlights the challenge of measuring the distributions of capacity directly. The results show that the distributions of capacity are skewed and can only be characterized through their second-moment properties. The study also highlights the challenge of measuring the distributions of fading

MG-GLAM, a cutting-edge N-body simulation software, was created to enhance the performance of the Grand Challenge N-body simulation by utilizing advanced algorithms and a novel tree construction method.  Developed by researchers at the San Diego Supercomputing Center, MG-GLAM builds upon previous codes such as Pegasus, LSH, and Harp, introducing a new approach to hierarchical grouping that reduces computational time and memory allocation.  Through optimization techniques and a highly optimized version of the SPG sorting algorithm, MG-GLAM achieved significant speed improvements, with a 3.5 factor increase in performance over its predecessors while reducing memory usage by 2.5 times.

We introduce the chordal stochastic Loewner evolution in multiple dimensions and show it is the same as the branching version of the Schramm-Loewner evolution. This involves analyzing driving processes and identifying the corresponding uniform convergence rates for the corresponding L^infty norms. The study of the chordal SLE also reveals an association with the program of constructing imaginary surfaces through complex analysis, specifically the potential theory approach introduced by Lennart Baker.

WorkingWiki is a specialized version of the typical wiki platform, designed to make available advanced functionality for the collaborative development of manuscripts and software. Unlike conventional wiki platforms based on MediaWiki, WorkingWiki's unique features include a built-in issue-tracking system, test data management, and tools for browsing and executing code. Additionally, it offers a more flexible configuration option in comparison to standard MediaWiki installations.

Multiple combustion theories including Eddy-Dissipation, Eddy-Break-Up, and Progress Variable models have been applied to complex turbulent reacting flows. Although these theories have been widely used, they are often based on arbitrary time-scale assumptions which can lead to inaccuracies in such applications. A new linearized analysis framework has been established to investigate turbulent reacting flows and this paper evaluates various combustion models within this framework. Numerical simulations were conducted to determine the model parameters and the results were compared to obtain the most suitable model. The study found that the Eddy-Dissipation model performed best and the parameters were obtained through a numerical simulation method.

Researchers have discovered a significant relationship between the acoustic-buoyant frequency and the behavior of waves in stars. When this frequency is high, they have found that the $\\ell=1$ p-modes are able to overcome the turbulent mixing barrier, while the 5-d modes are susceptible to it. However, the 2-g modes are unaffected by it. The team's analysis indicates a distinct resonance within a specific region of the star's interior, linked to its acoustic-buoyant frequency, which supports previous findings. The relationship between this frequency and the star's internal structure is complex, influenced by the interplay between gravity and sound waves, and is observable in p-modes, but is obscured in g-modes by the effects of angular momentum. The distinction between these modes of frequency and their respective roles in the star's evolution necessitates a reevaluation of the mixing barrier's impact, particularly in stars with low surface chemical enrichment, where the influence of the 5-d modes may be outweighed by that of the 2-g modes.

In complex systems, identifying the number of synchronized clusters can be challenging due to the presence of multiple coexisting patterns of synchronization. A new approach determines this number by analyzing the structure of stability for the system's synchronized states, leveraging the fact that only cluster-specific modes of synchronization are stable within each cluster. This approach is applicable to systems characterized by multiple coexistence states, including those with asynchronous bases, and provides a practical method for detecting clusters even in systems with an infinite number of synchronized states.

Our study examines the dynamics of nearest-neighbor dimers on triadic, diamond, and square lattices under temperature using molecular dynamics simulations and reveals distinct differences in their behavior. On the triadic and diamond lattices, dimers exhibit correlated and restricted motion compared to their counterparts on the square lattice, leading to distinct types of motion and associated dynamic properties. The triadic lattice demonstrates self-similar behavior in its motion and dynamic properties across varying temperatures, whereas the diamond lattice shows different dynamic properties compared to the self-similar triadic lattice and restricted lattices like the linear chain.

In the early universe, when neutrinos were in contact with dark matter, a specific type of dark matter, having a mass below a certain threshold, would experience an abrupt shift in its equilibrium state. This occurrence resulted in the overproduction of dark matter particles, leading to an excessive amount of relic density. The interconnection between this phenomenon and the fine-tuning problem associated with the Higgs mechanism becomes apparent when the ultralight dark matter is coupled to neutrinos. The interplay between this phenomenon and the cosmological evolution of neutrinos is examined, taking into consideration the constraints imposed by primordial nucleosynthesis, the current observations of large scale structure, and dark matter relic density. The outcome of this analysis reveals that the fine-tuning problem can be resolved through an alternative explanation, one that is independent of the Higgs mechanism.

The concept of Extremely High Energy (EHE) photons, predicted by Quantum Electrodynamics, remains a topic of debate due to a lack of direct observational evidence. Estimates suggest that the number of observable instances should be in the hundreds by now, yet none have been detected despite significant research efforts. A new analysis explores the properties of large groups of cosmic rays that could originate from EHE gamma-ray interactions with the interstellar medium, with a focus on their spatial patterns and potential observability. Findings show that while some CR ensembles might be identifiable as unusual distributions of arrival locations, others would appear similar to typical distribution patterns, resulting from the combination of various factors including the energy at which CR particles are produced, the path lengths over which CR particles persist, and the characteristics of the magnetic field that affects particle trajectories. As a result, the discovery of EHE gamma-rays through analysis of CR ensembles may be challenging and likely to require a more comprehensive approach that incorporates a broader understanding of CR phenomena.

A nonlocal gravity theory has been proposed, with a constitutive relation derived from an isotropic gradient approach, which is independent of reference frames andcorresponds to observable quantities such as curvature and their second derivatives. Problems with nonlocal cosmological perturbation theory were addressed by analyzing vector and scalar perturbations within a nonlocal gravity framework, with the results showing that nonlocality can resolve issues present in general relativity at the non-linear level, and the nonlocal Hubble ratio remains relatively constant across different nonlocal parameters during the evolution of the universe during the radiation-dominated and dark energy-dominated eras.

In our research, we developed a comprehensive design framework for Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) that combines principles of functional programming, type theory, and distributed systems. This framework, known as "Larida," offers a formal specification for designing and analyzing CRDTs through functional data structures, ensuring that Larida functions preserve data types and foster cooperation among replicated nodes. Building upon existing work by Shapiro and Baillargeon, we have successfully applied our framework to a range of prominent CRDT examples, including last seen values, multi-value sets, counters, registers, and conflict-free counters. By utilizing Larida's design principles, we have derived precise proofs for the convergence, anti-entropy methods, and replication semantics of these CRDTs.

To comprehend how new proteins influence existing phenotypes, it's essential to study the impact of protein sequences on uncharacterized SNPs associated with phenotypes. To achieve this, our research leverages vast amounts of sequence data, including 120 million protein sequences and 400,000 human phenotypes, and develops a method to analyze the effect of protein sequences on uncharacterized SNPs. By applying this method, we identified a considerable influence of protein sequences on a substantial number of phenotypes and found that their impact is primarily due to structural changes in proteins rather than sequence-based factors. Furthermore, we observed a considerable disparity in the influence of protein sequences on different traits, with the largest effects seen in traits related to immune system function, metabolism, and development. By predicting the function of thousands of uncharacterized proteins, we demonstrated the significance of protein sequences in determining the function of proteins with established functions.

The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC surveyed the creation of strange mesons in proton-proton collisions at energies of 13 TeV, a threshold previously explored at 7 and 8 TeV. When comparing production rates, a 10% increase was found, aligning with the expected enhancement resulting from gluon gluon interactions and the fragmentation of energetic gluons. The study of strange meson production over transverse momentum also revealed a rise in particle ratios, consistent with evolving energy dependencies in proton-proton collisions.

Our research reveals a 2 to 3 order of magnitude population disparity between neutron star Low Mass X-ray Binaries with accretion-driven X-ray emission and the overall population of millisecond radio pulsars within the Galaxy. This disparity challenges the long-held assumption that LMXBs and radio pulsars share a common birth rate. However, our findings suggest that the majority of LMXBs are likely disrupted without producing detectable radio pulsars. As a result, we estimate that between 68 to 92 percent of LMXBs experience this fate path. Furthermore, our research indicates that the total birth rate of LMXBs stands at roughly 0.32 per year within the Galaxy.

To determine one-dimensional velocity dispersion in wide binary star systems, radar observations can be used to enhance the accuracy of measurements. Using line velocities instead of line widths provides more precise results. A method to estimate one-dimensional velocity dispersion is typically based on line velocities, but can be limited by systematic errors. These errors stem from line shifts caused by line profiles and radial line velocities. A new approach to calculate one-dimensional velocity dispersion takes into account line velocities, line shifts, and line profiles. It is shown that this method significantly improves the accuracy of measurements by reducing systematic errors. The impact of line profile assumptions on the results is also examined, revealing a considerable effect of $10^{\frac{1-\sigma_{1D}^2}{2}}$ when using line widths instead of line velocities. Furthermore, an analysis of line velocity data from the M31Wide Binary Radar Survey shows that the velocity dispersion of line profiles is approximately 100 km/s. However, line profiles themselves play a crucial role in the determination of one-dimensional velocity dispersion. It is also argued that line profile assumptions should be matched to actual line profile observations to maintain physical consistency.

The relationship between the polarization properties of radio sources and the large-scale magnetic fields they inhabit is a crucial area of study. By analyzing 10333 radio sources from the Large Area Telescope (LAT) at energies between 100-300 MeV, using data from the Planck satellite and the WMAP satellite, we found a strong correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum and the median fractional polarization. This correlation suggests that more heavily polarized sources at higher frequencies have a stronger tendency to follow the curvature-polarization relationship. Furthermore, by analyzing the distribution of sources based on their polarization properties and spatial distribution within the sky, we found evidence for a tendency of highly polarized sources to concentrate in regions with strong magnetic fields, specifically in the outer regions of the Milky Way and in the Virgo cluster.

In one-dimensional flows, weak shocks typically transition to strong shocks due to the conversion of kinetic energy into heat, aided by the generation of vorticity. Our research reveals that this shock strengthening is accelerated by flow dispersion in multi-dimensional configurations, causing a different primary influence. In such scenarios, strong shocks can form even without vorticity generation, solely through the spread of flow components across orthogonal dimensions. This effect is illustrated through a simple numerical example, where a one-dimensional strong shock forms in a multi-dimensional flow, despite the initial conditions indicating no shock formation in one dimension.

We provide an illustration of a level M and weight k+1 Lissner-Newman Z_l-module isomorphism from M^2 Hecke algebra to (M^2 \o S_k(U(1)))_l Hecke algebra, extending the well-known Lissner-Newman isomorphism from weight k to level M Hecke algebras. This is achieved by a combination of local and global techniques, building upon the geometric modularity of multiple weights and the non-algebraic weight k+1 Lissner-Newman isomorphism. As a result, we derive a geometric modularity lifting theorem for non-algebraic weights, provided that a specific Lissner-Newman isomorphism exists for those weights.

To control complex chemical reactions, it is essential to identify and manipulate critical vibrational modes influencing the reaction barrier. A key concept, dynamic stabilization, suggests that by coupling a reaction mode to another vibrational mode with the right characteristics, one can stabilize the reaction barrier. Although this idea has been proposed before, the conditions required to achieve this effect have not been thoroughly explored. Using a model inspired by the HCN dimer, we investigate how the interaction between two vibrational modes affects the reaction barrier by adjusting their frequencies, coupling strength, and potential energy surfaces. Our analysis reveals that the shape of the potential energy surface plays a crucial role in dynamic stabilization. In some cases, coupling the modes of motion increases the height of the reaction barrier, while in other cases it lowers it. Surprisingly, we find that the conditions required to achieve dynamic stabilization are quite broad and can be easily achieved in many molecular systems. This insight suggests that the enhancement of reaction mode quantum states by coupling with other vibrational modes could be a general phenomenon, offering a new perspective on the control of chemical reactions.

Adachi-Iyama-Ishida's $au$-tilting theory was introduced in 2009 and has been a significant aspect of modern representation theory. Their work built upon Iyama's previous findings from 2005 and Mortsell's 2008 research, both heavily centered on $au$-tilting and its related concepts like Auslander-Reiten translation and tilted algebras. Since then, the method of applying $au$-tilting has become a crucial tool, used to derive multiple results, such as the classification of stable tubular algebras in 2010, the classification of strongly stable module trees in 2011, and the classification of strongly stable module varieties in 2014. This special issue is dedicated to Adachi-Iyama-Ishida's $au$-tilting theory on its tenth anniversary, featuring five new research papers that apply and extend its methods, encompassing topics like $au$-tilting pairs, module trees, module varieties, cluster tilting algebras, and domestic algebras.

To enhance the complexity of further dialogue responses, our approach leverages the semantics of preceding conversations to expand response R-1's semantic possibilities. In the existing method, cross-domain attention is used to combine the semantics of R and previous conversations P, but this may lead to response R's semantics being overshadowed. In contrast, our proposed attention-free mixing technique prioritizes the semantics of P over R, resulting in a generated response whose semantic diversity surpasses the baseline. Furthermore, our model exhibits improved performance in generating responses with elevated semantic diversity, according to the results of experiments conducted on the Dialogstate 5 dataset.

Autonomous driving systems rely on efficient video analysis to navigate complex situations. Ongoing changes in traffic patterns necessitate a robust assistance system that adapts quickly to new circumstances. Current approaches to recognizing actions from raw video feed are hindered by several limitations, including the need for extensive labeled data, inflexible action classes, and an inability to account for contextual information. We introduce an end-to-end machine learning framework that learns to identify actions and their contextual significance from labeled data alone, allowing it to operate with a high degree of flexibility in response to new data. By processing raw video inputs and leveraging contextual information, our model learns to recognize actions and its learned representations exhibit a high degree of robustness in the face of various distortions. We evaluate our approach by subjecting it to a range of challenges, including real-world data, and demonstrate its superiority over alternative methods.

Hydrogen burning in low-mass stars and planets is influenced by angular momentum, which also affects the onset of gravitational contraction and central temperature. A specific threshold of angular momentum exists beyond which the hydrogen burning pattern changes drastically. This study re-examines this threshold for various mass ranges and finds that it remains relatively constant at approximately 1.5 x 10^18 gyros/s^(1/2) for masses between 0.1 and 0.6 solar masses. However, this research uncovers an unexpected consequence of exceeding this threshold - a sharp increase in the minimum central temperature required for hydrogen burning, accompanied by a significant rise in luminosity across all mass ranges. As a result, objects with angular momenta greater than this threshold will experience reduced hydrogen burning rates, leading to shorter lifetimes. Objects with initial angular momenta above this threshold will also experience increased cooling ages due to their higher surface luminosity. Additionally, this research reveals that objects with initial angular momenta greater than this threshold will be placed on the Hertzsprung-Hertzprung diagram above the main sequence, resulting in misidentification as sub-stellar objects.

To compensate for falling statistics of certain $\tau$ decay modes, such as $\tau^- \to K_S \pi^0 \nu_\tau$, artificial neural networks can be utilized to interpolate missing energy from a set of visible final-state particles, thereby enhancing the precision of invariant mass calculations. By employing a large dataset containing $84.3$ picobarns of $\tau$ data, we have determined the most effective way to employ neural networks to accomplish this goal, and have found that their usage yields a 20-fold improvement in mass resolution compared to traditional methods, along with a 500-fold decrease in systematic error when the interpolated energy falls outside the $E_{\text{visible}}$ range of $0$ to $30$ GeV.

A unified approach to describing ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic gamma-ray burst afterglows in external magnetic fields is introduced. This model builds upon established theories, rectifying their limitations. It is observed that prior models exhibit unphysical behavior in ultra-relativistic scenarios or fail to account for the interplay between relativistic and non-relativistic parameters in magnetic fields. In contrast, the new framework seamlessly bridges the two regimes, providing a coherent description of afterglows across all relativistic speeds.

In graph theory, identifying the fewest number of vertices to split simultaneously is crucial in achieving a planar embedding. This concept is particularly important for bipartite graphs, which often require planar drawings that minimize edge crossings and split only necessary vertices. By examining a specific type of bipartite graph known as a grid graph, researchers have previously established a specific splitting pattern that can break the $O(|E|)$ barrier. However, this particular approach is only applicable to a specific subclass of grid graphs. In this study, a new approach is presented that provides a more general solution for splitting vertices for all bipartite grid graphs, requiring a number of splits proportional to the number of edges, and is accompanied by an efficient algorithm for implementing this method.

Deep learning models have achieved high accuracy, but they often struggle with a critical issue: achieving calibration when dealing with data imbalance. The primary goal of this research is to thoroughly assess the effectiveness of score calibration techniques in tackling classification imbalance. We examined and compared the performance of four score calibration methods, specifically perturbation-based, regression-based, temperature scaling, and vector normalization approaches. The results of our experiments revealed that the methods' performances vary significantly, with some performing well in certain scenarios but poorly in others. Notably, the best-performing methods outperformed non-calibrated models in some cases, achieving a 10-20% reduction in error rates. Furthermore, we identified that the best method depends on the specific scenario, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting a score calibration technique for data imbalance classification.

To improve bipedal locomotion, we employed an advanced optimization approach called direct collocation with nonlinear programming. This method allowed us to build a fast closed-loop feedback controller, which quickly reflected changes during gait cycles. By combining feedback control with the optimized gait patterns, we achieved a significant reduction in energy expenditure and an improvement in walking speed. The closed-loop control helped to mitigate the negative effects of slow feedback response during gait cycles, particularly the loss of speed.

The paper proves that for a power series field with an infinite ground field, decidability of the theory involving a total residue map is equivalent to the decidability of its associated algebraic theory.

Researchers have discovered various web applications that are vulnerable to Flush+Reload attacks, which can be executed even if the target memory region cannot be directly accessed. However, these attacks face a significant limitation due to the time-consuming nature of flushing and reloading memory. As a result, they require a large number of traces and a coarser time granularity, which can complicate the adjustment of timing windows. To address this issue, the HyperDegrade technique is introduced, which significantly enhances the efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks by reducing the time granularity from hundreds of milliseconds to as little as 0.16 seconds, and by decreasing the number of required traces from hundreds to as little as 10 traces for certain web applications. The hyper-degrading memory access pattern allows for the detection of memory modifications made several seconds apart, which is demonstrated using a custom-built measurement tool called HyperDrain. The results of the evaluation show that HyperDegrade is highly effective in detecting memory modifications across various web applications and scenarios.

A recent study published in the journal Physical Review Letters reports that the value of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment remains unexplained after the inclusion of lattice quantum chromodynamics data. This discrepancy could be resolved by introducing New Physics at a relatively low scale of around 100-300 MeV, which is remarkably close to its original predicted value. This finding holds significance as it indicates that the introduction of New Physics to explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron is still feasible, despite the inclusion of updated lattice data for quantum field theories. This development may prompt researchers to re-examine experiments with a focus on the associated $d$-wave scalar form factor. Furthermore, a similar discrepancy in the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon cannot be ruled out and would have substantial implications for ongoing and future experiments involving rare processes in quantum field theories.

To determine the fundamental parameters of the Standard Model, precise measurements of tree-level processes such as $K^0 \to \ell^+\ell^-$, $B^0 \to K^0 \ell^+\ell^-$, and $B^0_s \to K^0_\mathbf{S} \ell^+\ell^-$ are crucial. Global theoretical predictions for these decays have been recalursively reevaluated to incorporate the latest developments in $B$ and $K$ anatomy and to ensure consistency with the Global Electroweak Working Group's recommendations. Theoretical uncertainties in $K^0 \to \ell^+\ell^-$ and $B^0 \to K^0 \ell^+\ell^-$ have been significantly reduced to less than 1%, while the estimate for $B^0_s \to K^0_\mathbf{S} \ell^+\ell^-$ has been revised to reduce its uncertainty to less than 2%, primarily due to an updated treatment of $m_t$ and $\alpha_s$ uncertainties in the $N_s$ contributions.

A new set of transformations has been defined for generalised diagrams representing links and knots, comprising horizontal and diagonal changes. It was proven that these diagonal shifts enable conversion between a link diagram and any other link diagram representing the same topological structure, also establishing that horizontal and diagonal transformations are equivalent in terms of allowing a diagram to be transformed into any other diagram with the same underlying topological structure.

Given a finite harmonic morphism $f: X \to Y$ between tropical curves and a rational function $r$ on $X$, whose kernel does not intersect any component of $X$, the pull-back $f^r: k(X) \to k(Y)$ induces an extension of the semifield of fractions on $Y$ to the semifield of fractions on $X$. Notably, this pull-back is non-constant whenever $f$ is surjective. Furthermore, there exists a unique tropical curve $X'$ and harmonic morphism $f': X' \to X$ such that $f'^{r'} = f \circ f^{r^{-1}}$ for some rational function $r'$ on $X'$, whose kernel does not intersect any component of $X'$.

We offer an innovative method for calculating a particular combination of cocycles that produce combinations of knot invariants, including Jones polynomial, knot determinant, and the A-polynomial. Furthermore, this approach reveals a connection among these invariants, expressing one as another divided by the cocycle combination. The coccycle combination can be represented through a modified version of its basic components, allowing its own study. This has implications for understanding the invariants themselves. Building upon this, if the coccycle combinations are torsion-free, we can determine the invariants' properties based on that of the coccycles alone.

The standard three-neutrino mixing model is examined in the context of stellar stability. We demonstrate that the current white dwarf and neutron star stability, along with constraints from other areas, necessitates extremely small masses for two of the neutrinos. However, if we consider a fourth neutrino state, this condition becomes less stringent, and this state's mass can be comparable to the masses of the other two. As a result, the distinction between "light" and "heavy" neutrinos is no longer clear-cut. We also explore the implications of this scenario for lepton number non-conservation in the early universe.

Open-source computer programs that execute matrix commands have experienced a significant boost in performance due to the use of parallel computing techniques. To further enhance their speed, developers are utilizing specialized hardware like GPUs and CPUs with built-in math engines to perform matrix calculations. A novel method for rapidly multiplying large matrices on laptops and desktops has been developed, utilizing lightweight software to split matrices and allocate specific sections to the math engines, thereby speeding up matrix multiplication. A notable increase in performance was observed, with matrices up to 15000 by 15000 able to be multiplied in under one second.

In a multi-agent task environment, agents must decide whether to tackle existing tasks or wait for new tasks to emerge, which is an optimal decision-making problem known as Multi-Agent Wait Problem (MAWP). Current methods address MAWP by solving an equation directly, but these methods fail to consider the inherent variability in task generation and instead treat it as a deterministic process. In contrast, our novel approach to solving MAWP treats task generation as a stochastic process. We achieve this by casting the system's task generation process as a renewal process and by utilizing the resulting variables in our solution equation. Through numerical examples and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our method accurately reflects the true distribution of waiting times and outperforms traditional methods, especially in scenarios with significant variability.

To achieve a deeper understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and forces at the quantum level, precise predictions are essential. Given the upcoming construction of cutting-edge colliders such as CLIC, FCC-hh, LHC, LHeC, ILC, VLHC, CEPC, CSC, ICR, and PS, significant advancements in theoretical precision strategies are necessary. Leveraging existing research, we outline a comprehensive framework that utilizes a multistage approach to achieve precise predictions, incorporating a combination of automatic tools and human interventions at different levels. Specifically, we recommend utilizing a multilevel framework that consists of four stages: (1) experimental data interpretation, (2) cross-section precision, (3) parton distribution function evolution, and (4) phenomenological analysis. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of developing robust automatic tools for each stage, ensuring that the output is processable and reliable for further human analysis. By adopting this multilevel framework, we believe that we can effectively address the theoretical precision challenges facing these new colliders.

This research proves the feasibility of outsourced FL servers being exploited to reveal users' private information. We've successfully developed practical methods for two prominent VFL learning algorithms, hinge loss-based classification and squared loss-based linear regression. Furthermore, our experiments validate the efficacy of these attacks in extracting sensitive data across various scenarios. The research highlights the vulnerabilities inherent to FL systems and emphasizes the importance of securing not just clients, but also servers, to protect user privacy.

We introduce Pseudo-Random Fourier Features (PRFF), an efficient technique for reducing the dimensionality of random Fourier features while maintaining their predictive accuracy. By drawing on the orthogonality of the Fourier transform, PRFF fine-tunes the weights of a subset of features to mimic the behavior of the original reduced features, thereby achieving a method for dimensionality reduction that is both theoretically justified and practically effective. In experiments, PRFF outperforms the method of Random Fourier Features in a range of applications, including kernel ridge regression, support vector machines, and deep learning.

This survey paper leverages higher geometry to reevaluate regular group actions, 
diagonal groups, and the Cartesian Decomposition Theorem. By extending basic 
properties of group actions and diagonal groups, we demonstrate the significance 
of these concepts across various mathematical frameworks, including differential 
geometry, algebraic geometry, and differential algebra. The proof of the 
Cartesian Decomposition Theorem is then presented in a simplified, general form. 
The techniques employed ensure the validity of this decomposition for multiple 
group actions, including those on affine spaces, differential affine spaces, 
differential algebra sets, and algebraic sets.

This study formulates the minimal M\"obius scalar curvature theorem for compact conformally flat hypersurfaces in space-like M\"obius manifolds in $n$ dimensions, establishing a lower bound condition for this curvature expression in terms of an energy-related term and a surface tension term, specifically $\frac{R_{M}^{2}}{n-1} \geq \frac{6(n-1)}{n^2-4} E_M + \frac{8(n-1)(n-2)}{n^2-4} E_{\tilde{\gamma}}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Willmore conformal immersions satisfy this lower bound condition, and that it is sharp for all natural numbers.

Automated cardiac image segmentation using deep learning techniques has shown high accuracy when tested on datasets containing a limited range of heart conditions. Nevertheless, the reliability of these models in handling a diverse range of pathologies across the whole spectrum remains unclear. To address this uncertainty, we conducted an extensive analysis of multiple models, including ENZO, a highly successful segmentation network, by subjecting them to a broad range of cases, including common and rare heart defects, as outlined in the ACDC and MIMIC datasets. The evaluation of these models revealed a significant discrepancy between their performance on easy cases and harder cases, with a large variation in errors of up to 25% EPE. Furthermore, we observed that the error patterns of the models were distinct, with some behaving consistently across different conditions and others exhibiting significant variability. The results of our analysis indicated that the models performed better on areas affected by scarring and dilation but struggled with regions affected by tumors and other mass lesions. The findings of our study provide valuable insights into the performance of cardiac image segmentation models and their limitations, which can inform clinical applications and guide the development of more robust models in the future.

We've developed a new approach to describe small-scale oscillations in materials with heterogeneous damage by combining gradient damage models and a multiple-scale method. By dividing the material into small regions and analyzing each one separately, we've identified a key factor that causes oscillations: an imbalance between the rates at which damage spreads and the rates at which energy dissipates. This imbalance creates an effect where damage appears to shift back and forth, and we've found that it only affects areas that are smaller than a certain critical size. We've also found that this approach can be simplified to focus on the most rapidly changing areas of the material, and this simplification leads to a more efficient and easier-to-solve mathematical problem. By applying these techniques to a common type of elastic damage model, we've found that they help to eliminate oscillations and produce more realistic results.

In the context of Fast Fading and an unlimited number of users, a new energy-efficient method called Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique is proposed for SWIPT-enabled networks, resulting in a significant enhancement of Energy Efficiency Ratio with minimal increase in Power Consumption Ratio. Analysis and the application of an optimization method known as Successive Harmonic Mean method enables determination of optimal GAST parameters, leading to further increased efficiency gains. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing solutions such as ON/OFF technique, DAST, and the standard Hybrid method.

Recent foundation models like Foundation Models for Object Detection (FMOD) have achieved notable success in the area of object detection.  However, the existing FMOD-based methods still face challenges when it comes to detecting objects of different sizes.  This issue is largely because the backbone networks used in these methods are trained on large objects and don't perform as well on smaller objects.  To address this problem, we propose a new approach called Adaptive Foundation Models for Object Detection (AFMOD) that utilizes a feature pyramid network (FPN) to combine high-level context information from the foundation models while keeping the ability to learn discriminative local features for each scale.  A- FMOD leverages two strategies:  weighted fusion (WF) that allows for the adjustment of the weight of each feature map based on the object size, and channel permutation (CP) that enables the rearrangement of channels for better performance.  Through extensive experiments on the COCO dataset, A-FMOD shows superior performance over the existing FMOD-based methods and achieves competitive results with the state-of-the-art methods.  For example, A-FMOD achieves an mAP of 60.2% (+0.4% improvement) on the validation set of the COCO dataset with strong scaling.

Researchers have previously developed methods for estimating the distribution of a variable given its sufficient statistics, but these methods are limited to a specific type of statistical model. A new approach has been devised for a broader range of models, including those that are not explicitly defined, based on the concept of conditional bivariate exponential tails. This approach utilizes a specific set of assumptions about the statistical model's behavior and a specific formula to estimate the conditional bivariate tail distribution. The estimated distribution exhibits the same characteristics as the original variable's tail distribution, and it is possible to derive a specific formula for estimating the tail distribution in a specific type of statistical model.

Understanding natural language requires grasping various elements such as context, syntax, and vocabulary. Yet, significant variations in word forms can make it difficult for machines to process language. For instance, words ending in "-able" have distinct meanings based on their context, posing a challenge for machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, words with similar spellings yet differing meanings pose another classification problem. To address these complexities, this study proposes a method to generate context-specific words ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-ableable-able

Human conversational skills allow for the understanding of complex, unordered instructions that incorporate multiple forms of information. In contrast, current machine learning models, while capable of processing ordered lists of instructions, still significantly trail humans in this regard. To bridge this gap, we've developed a new task called "Conversational Sequence-Level Reasoning" (CSLR) that enables the accurate sequencing and use of unordered multimodal information for task-based applications. Evaluating this model using both automatic evaluation metrics and human assessment tools shows a notable improvement when comparing models that do and do not utilize sequence-level information. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating attention mechanisms and source encoding aids in achieving high performance.

In complex networks, the distribution of component sizes resulting from random failures or immunization can skew heavily towards smaller components. This skewness hinders the effective dissemination of information or influence across the network. We've developed a novel method to enhance network resilience by fragmenting the network into larger components. Specifically, we investigated the effect of removing a single node from a network and defined a weighted distribution based on the resulting component sizes. When applied to an undirected and unweighted network, this distribution is equivalent to the standard component size distribution. We found that an exponential function accurately fits this standard distribution for most networks. The average component size is proportional to the square root of the network size, explaining previous observations of skewed component sizes in complex networks. We further demonstrated that removing a large component can lead to a significant increase in the next component size, indicating a potential influence on the standard distribution shape. We also found that networks with similar standard component size distributions can differ significantly in their structure.

Rajasekhar in arXiv found a new point process corresponding to the generalized sextic Freud weight and proved the corresponding universality result holding for a specific scaling limit when compared to the generalized Airy weight, which has a different expression of $x^4$ instead of $x^6$ for similar purposes. The generalized sextic Freud weight is defined as $w(x)=x^{\beta_2}\left(\sum_{j=1)^6 x^r_{(j)}\right)^{\beta_1}$ where $x_{(1)}\ge x_{(2)}\ge \ldots \ge x_{(6)}$ and the resulting point process and measure also have specific expressions based on the generalized sextic Freud weight. The associated equilibrium measure, point process and corresponding determinantal point process measures can be expressed through the Mhaskar-Nazarov-Panov generalization of the Fyodorov-Huh-Soshika formula. The required statistical properties of the equilibrium measure, point process and corresponding determinantal point process measures also enable proof of the required universality result holding for a specific scaling limit when compared to the generalized Airy weight. The required proof of the relevant properties and the corresponding universality result holding for a specific scaling limit when compared to the generalized Airy weight involves complex calculations and applications of various mathematical expressions and theorems.

A novel design called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is presented, which significantly boosts the sensitivity of interferometers by leveraging the amplification effects of sloshing modes in liquid-filled cavities. By comparing this design to conventional Sagnac, Michelson, and torsion pendulum setups, it becomes clear that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers the highest sensitivity improvement. The sloshing-Sagnac design enhances sensitivity by taking advantage of the large responsivity of sloshing modes in liquid-filled cavities. However, this benefit comes with a cost, as the sensitivity gain is achieved at the expense of much slower response times. A simple liquid-filled sloshing-Sagnac design is also presented, which could potentially utilize existing Michelson Sagnac interferometer infrastructure.

In this research, we propose a novel random access protocol called NOVR-XL for XL-MIMO systems and analyze its performance under various conditions, followed by an optimization method to minimize collision probability. Additionally, we present an optimized protocol called NOVR-XL-RA and mathematically analyze its performance, showing significant improvements over traditional protocols. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical findings, revealing a notable increase in access success probability and system throughput.

The formation of protoplanetary disks is a complex process, and researchers are still debating how a disk's structure and composition evolve during its formation stages. A key aspect of this process is the formation of small particles, or planetesimals, which are crucial for creating terrestrial planets through further gravitational accumulation. Researchers have long believed that a disk's faint emission in the microwave range is a sign of warm dust located near its center. However, a recent study suggests that this dust may not be a significant indicator of a disk's evolution into a planetary system. Instead, the formation of a disk's solid structures, such as cavities, rings, and spirals, plays a more important role in the creation of planetesimals. These structures form when a disk's solid particles collide and stick together, eventually becoming larger bodies that orbit the star in a specific pattern. By analyzing data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and the Spitzer Space Telescope, researchers found that a disk's solid structures are a key indicator of a system's potential to create terrestrial planets.

A novel energy density functional called the BigAppleDF has been created and its strength and saturation properties are examined. Calculations of binding energies, radii, and neutron skins are also performed for a range of nuclei. The results show a strong similarity to those obtained with the well-known UNIQFD functional. Furthermore, the neutron skin thickness of $158$ pm for $^{78}$Ni has been determined, consistent with value predicted by the UNIQFD. The characteristics of BigAppleDF, in particular its nonempirical nature, make it an attractive alternative to the widely used density functionals like UNIQFD.

Using exact diagonalization to solve a single-band Hubbard model on a cubic lattice, we have determined the spectral characteristics of SrMnO$_3$ for both correlated and uncorrelated orbitals. The results show that when the effects of correlation are considered, the spectral structure undergos a significant change, with the appearance of a prominent hump near the Fermi level. This hump is reduced in intensity or disappears when the influence of the on-site interaction is limited to a single orbital. The associated mass renormalization is also examined in relation to the correlation between adjacent electrons.

We created a variety of Molmer-Sorensen gates that are resistant to frequency variations, using a shared atomic frequency as a reference for both applied lights, and compared the entanglement generation of these gates on ion lattices using the Hamiltonian's SU(2) symmetry. By optimizing the difference in frequencies between the lights, we reduced the required duration of robust gate implementation by a factor of up to 10 while maintaining the same level of entanglement. Our findings suggest that implementing robust coherent atomic interferometry could be feasible using optical transitions near atomic resonance.

Using a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental data, the relationship between the structure and B-cation positioning within perovskites has been extensively studied. Contrary to a previously held assumption, the equilibrium volume within these compounds does not directly correlate with B-cation displacement when considering a range of fillers. Instead, both volume and filler have independent effects on B-cation positioning. B-cations in larger volumes tend to displace further from their equilibrium positions, while those in smaller volumes show reduced displacement. Additionally, the choice of filler influences B-cation positioning, with certain fillers enhancing displacement in certain volumes and hindering it in others. A comprehensive database consisting of over 1300 compositions has been utilized in this analysis, allowing for an in-depth examination of the interplay between volume, filler, and B-cation positioning within perovskites.

Researchers believe the recently discovered compound GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ has a 3D honeycomb structure, which induces unusual Dirac electrons and promising many-body physics phenomena. To better understand its properties, a theoretical lattice model was created using a first-principles method called DFT. Further analysis of this model revealed that interactions between electrons could lead to the creation of exotic states such as a topological insulator, a Dirac semimetal, or a magnetic material with a non-trivial gap. Researchers propose that GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ is a good candidate for a magnetic topological insulator or a ferromagnetic Dirac semimetal. These predicted properties make this compound theoretically interesting and worthy of further experimental study.

A new bimodal beta distribution has been developed, addressing the limitations of existing double-sided beta distributions in handling data with clear left and right modes. This novel distribution distinguishes itself from the four previous double-sided beta distributions through its unique probability density function and random variable generation method. Notably, bimodality in data is often characterized by distinct modes rather than weights on the main mass, leading to a potential misunderstanding of the terminology. Properties of the new distribution have been explored, including its first moment, a modified version applicable to negative data, and a special case leading to the exponential distribution. Furthermore, the distribution's performance has been evaluated through simulations, and it has been compared to other double-sided distributions using real-world datasets.

The search for heavy neutral leptons at the LHC is a significant area of research, with the goal of understanding why neutrinos have such low masses. Due to their weak interaction with other particles, HNLs have a long lifetime, allowing them to travel a significant distance before decaying. As a result, they can originate from the early universe or quark-gluon plasma created during heavy ion collisions and reach the LHC detectors. To enhance the sensitivity for HNL production in the hadronization process, the LHC can be paired with event generators that simulate the interaction between partons and the vacuum, in addition to interactions influenced by QCD. This study compares the HNL production cross-sections across various event generators, taking into account the characteristics of the LHC and its detectors. The results show that the production rates vary significantly, depending on the specific generator used, across different kinematic regions. However, the overall expectations are consistent with existing experimental limits. To improve the detection capabilities in future experiments, the LHC will need to achieve lower background levels or employ more sensitive detection methods.

We re-examine the operation of a Sagnac interferometer under conditions of ultrafast laser interactions, considering the effects of relativistic Doppler shifts on light traveling in opposite directions. Our analysis indicates that a previously reported phenomenon, in which counter-propagating light beams induce a shift away from resonance, is actually an overstatement. Instead, we find that the shift is the same for both beams and thus cancels out. Notably, this cancellation is independent of the specific velocity of light in the moving frame. However, we do identify a circumstance under which the shift differs between the two beams - when the frame of reference is aligned with the direction of propagation. In this situation, the shift causes a frequency shift from resonance, and this effect could potentially be utilized for the generation of ultrafast pulses.

We challenge a longstanding conjecture that a nilfibre cannot be dominated by a dense subgroup of a fibre. Contrary to this, we present an example of a group G, an action of G on a space X, a subgroup H of G, and a point x in X, such that the nilfibre X//H contains a dense H-orbit within the rational tangent space, demonstrating that current techniques are insufficient to derive this contradiction from our construction.

Deep neural language models have significantly boosted performance in various language tasks like machine translation, text classification, and summarization. By leveraging the distributional hypothesis, $n$-gram models have been shown to be a simple yet effective technique that can enhance the performance of neural models when tested on tasks like machine translation and summarization. This paper delves into the benefits of combining $n$ gram models and neural language models, proposing CMixLM, a novel model that integrates the strengths of both. CMixLM initially employs a neural language model to predict future tokens based on past context, and then employs an $n$-gram model to rank candidate tokens and select the most probable one. This novel approach is evaluated on machine translation, text classification, and summarization tasks, demonstrating a notable improvement of up to 2.5 WAP for machine translation and outperforming all previous works combining neural models and $n$-gram models by a margin of 0.8-2.3 WAP.

Goulart and Huh previously proposed a connection between the mutation classes of Laurent polynomials and Fano 3-dimensional varieties. This paper builds upon their work by creating a comprehensive map that covers all mutation classes of Laurent polynomials in a specific 3-dimensional space, and further shows this map is bijective with respect to a particular equivalence relation. Furthermore, this relationship can be extended to a broader space of mutation classes accompanied by a linear form, resulting in a cover or a bijective map depending on the choice of parameters.

Reconstructing a three-dimensional face from multiple views is a well-known problem in computer vision, and previous studies have typically addressed it by analyzing face variations due to pose. In contrast, our proposed Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) innovatively tackles this challenge by distinguishing between pose-dependent and pose-independent factors and regressing them separately. By doing so, it can assemble a 3D face from these factors, regardless of the input images being from the same pose. In our experiments, our method consistently outperformed existing methods on two datasets, and our unique factor decomposition also enabled us to achieve impressive results in tasks such as face relighting and aging.

We have investigated the electronic properties of a model with a finite charge density at half-filling, and found that fractons, which typically have restricted mobility, can move freely within the system despite the finite charge. However, their ability to move long distances is impeded by a factor of (k_F/lamda)^2, where k_F is the wave number associated with the average charge density and lambda is the localization length of the charges. This restriction is shown to influence the movement of fractons only at very low temperatures, and can be understood in terms of a duality between the fracton and a boson with the same properties, which becomes pinned by the finite charge density. This results in an effective action that includes a mass term for the fracton, but only within a region of size lambda.

A notable issue in the study of the primordial curvature power spectrum arises from the fact that certain models of multi-field inflation can produce abnormally large, negative values of the Bardeen potential. This problem has been largely sidestepped in recent analyses due to the non-causality problem associated with the evolution of the Bardeen potential in the context of a given scalar power spectrum. Nonetheless, we have discovered that the scalar power spectrum plays a crucial role in determining the distribution of the Bardeen potential, particularly when the relevant perturbation theory parameters exhibit non-negligible variations across different scales of the cosmological horizon. Consequently, we have developed an approach to directly derive the probability density function of the Bardeen potential from the scalar power spectrum, and our results indicate that the conventional slow-roll inflationary predictions are indeed incorrect, with a significant proportion of Bardeen potential values falling within the range of $-10\lesssim\Phi\lesssim10$. Researchers are comparing the number of deepest nodes in two types of ordered trees: those with a standard structure and those with additional marked nodes. The ratio of their comparisons reveals an interesting pattern, indicating that the majority of standard trees contain exactly one deepest node, whereas marked trees often contain more than one deepest node. Further analysis shows that the average number of deepest nodes in marked trees is nearly twice as high as in standard trees. Additionally, the distribution of the number of deepest nodes in marked trees can be represented by a skew normal curve, providing a new insight into these trees.

Accurate optical character recognition is crucial in vote tabulation, and a key factor is the correction of printing irregularities, or spelling errors, that impede OCR success. We've developed a spell checking algorithm that leverages a modified version of the Levenshtein distance to compare and correct misspelled words, and its effectiveness is evident in its ability to improve the accuracy of OCR across various font types. In particular, it excels at correcting words whose prefix matches the spelling of another word, a common source of error in the voting process.

In the training of linear models with infinite-dimensional data, featuring a parameterized design that changes over time according to a continuous schedule, traditional methods face challenges. To overcome this, we propose an algorithm that employs a second-order unconstrained optimization method and takes advantage of the smooth nature of the schedule to achieve a significant reduction in computational costs per iteration. The algorithm is particularly well-suited for over-parameterized schedules and can produce an accurate solution that achieves the optimal rate of convergence with a small number of iterations. The method is also robust to various types of scheduling irregularities, such as abrupt changes, and can provide a solution with a near-optimal rate of convergence in the finite-dimensional case. The algorithm is supported by theoretical guarantees and has a clear connection to the classical method of conjugate gradients.

A novel bidirectional attention-based architecture has been introduced for the joint enhancement of multiple microphones' signals, and our research demonstrates its effectiveness in low-noise speech enhancement. Distinguished from other methods that solely employ forward or lateral attention, our proposed approach leverages bidirectional attention to counterbalance noise from various directions. Notably, our technique has shown substantial gains over alternative methods, including the original architecture, PASE, and D-TF-ASE, as verified through objective metrics. Furthermore, our method has a significant advantage in terms of mean opinion score (MOS), achieving the highest score of 3.79, which is a 0.14 improvement over the baseline and a 0.15 enhancement over PASE.

The safety of aircraft without regard to speed can be compromised if pressure sensors are hacked, potentially leading to catastrophic consequences. This research focuses on differential pressure sensors used in modern aircraft, particularly the LPTPS-100 model, which is similar to the sensors employed in the Boeing 787. By manipulating the pressure readings, hackers can exploit this vulnerability. Using a combination of evolutionary algorithms and a nonlinear feedforward learning method, a sophisticated attack was designed to deceive the defense system. Initial findings revealed that the attack succeeded in bypassing the protection mechanism on the LPTPS-100 model differential pressure sensors. Furthermore, the attack was adaptable to work on other similar sensors, such as those produced by the Honeywell model.

As the transition to low-carbon energy occurs, managing storage units that behave risk-aversely in response to uncertain future outcomes will become increasingly crucial. We've developed an equilibrium framework that accounts for risk-averse storage units within a general stochastic process setting, ensuring that expected utility losses don't exceed a given threshold. We apply this framework to analyze a specific case study involving a single-sided multi-participant system, where storage units compete for power dispatch opportunities. We find that an equilibrium solution exists and can be found through a process of marginalization, allowing us to analyze equilibrium behavior in comparison to several key scenarios. Notably, we observe that when storage units are risk-averse, they tend to avoid taking risks, often leading to suboptimal use of their generation and flexibility, with implications for policy decisions that aim to balance economic efficiency with the management of risk in energy systems.

To study the ultrafast structural changes in molecules following x-ray excitation, x-ray pulses must match core-excited state energies. Research using x-ray scattering and absorption, combined with theoretical analysis, has shown that tuning the energy of an x-ray pulse to match a specific core-excited state results in coherent electron motion within that state. A new study using x-ray scattering and absorption, along with theoretical analysis, reveals that altering the energy of an x-ray pulse to match a specific core-excited state results in the creation of a sideband in the spectrum, corresponding to a coherent electron motion between different core-excited states. This sideband was observed in formamide, a small organic molecule, and occurred within a time frame of less than one femtosecond. The energy difference between these states was found to be around 0.2 electron volts.

Mars' atmosphere was studied during a hypothetical Earth-like era when the atmosphere was thick and warm, thanks to a stable carbon dioxide cycle. Researchers analyzed how baroclinic storms behave in this environment and discovered striking similarities with the circulation patterns found in Earth's atmosphere. Additionally, they found that a stable carbon dioxide cycle is plausible if the atmosphere is present for an extended period, as it would maintain a balance of gas release from the surface, atmospheric circulation, and polar ice caps.

Current active learning methodologies, though effective for smaller datasets like CIFAR-10 and MNIST, fall short when dealing with large-scale datasets like ImageNet. To bridge this gap, we introduce BALD+, a novel, efficient and simple-to-implement algorithm that excels in selecting the most informative samples across various datasets of varying sizes. Unlike traditional methods, BALD+ doesn't require repeated queries to the model or extensive refinement of its suggestions. Instead, it directly chooses the most diverse samples that can reduce the remaining uncertainty after selection. We enhance the basic BALD algorithm by adding a maximum diversity constraint, making it suitable for large-scale datasets, and demonstrate the advantages of BALD+ through thorough experiments on datasets like ImageNet, CIFAR-10, MNIST, and WebVision.

Researchers have been trying to find a suitable replacement for the algebraic multiplicity of a matrix relative to a linear operator, in a way that it aligns with the principles of the Klein operator-based approach introduced by Gantel. Building upon this idea, we have developed a novel concept of generalized algebraic multiplicity that is closely related to the Schur operator. This new notion is particularly valuable as it enables the derivation of precise formulas for calculating the generalized algebraic multiplicity in instances where the algebraic multiplicity is infinite.

We investigate a variety of squeezing resources, including two-mode squeezing, triple-mode squeezing, and squeezing in different mode correlations, for enhancing optical phase sensing using homodyne measurements. By examining the sensitivity of these sensing systems, we identify two-mode squeezing as particularly effective and explain its benefits in terms of resource efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using two-mode squeezing and performing appropriate homodyne measurements can exploit quantum effects to surpass classical sensitivity by applying the right transformation. This strategy takes advantage of existing two-mode squeezing generation techniques, such as using parametric amplifiers or nonlinear optical processes, to enhance sensing performance.

To build a large-scale quantum computing system, reliable and controllable two-qubit logic operations are necessary. Leveraging spin-spring physics in silicon semiconductor quantum dots can provide the necessary scalability and control. A crucial step in this process is isolating the interaction between qubits by creating a barrier using nearby donor atoms. Studies have shown that the placement and adjustment of these donor atoms have a significant impact on the performance of two-qubit logic gates. Using a classical model, we investigate how the position and tuning of these donor atoms affect their performance under various conditions, including different tunnel couplings and photon interactions. Our findings indicate that the optimal placement and tuning of the donor atoms depend on the specific conditions of the qubit pair, and must be precisely controlled to achieve high fidelity. However, we also discovered that over the range of parameters that result in high fidelity, there is significant degeneracy in the optimal configurations, allowing for a degree of tolerance in placement and tuning.

In highly resistant quantum wells, we've discovered a persistent oscillation near the zero Landau level, missing in larger samples. This phenomenon is explained by scattering from edge states and can be adjusted with a gate. Similar behavior is observed in quantum Hall nematics and graphene. In contrast, bulk electron populations exhibit scattering-dominated patterns. These findings highlight the distinction between bulk and edge behavior in these systems.

This research paper proposes an adaptive cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (AC-NOMA) protocol that dynamically chooses between cooperative and non-cooperative modes based on the number of users in the system, with the aim of minimizing an outage probability criterion. We derive an analytical formula to calculate the outage probability of this adaptive system and through numerical simulations, demonstrate its superior performance compared to fixed cooperative NOMA, cooperative orthogonal multiple access, and non-cooperative NOMA systems in terms of outage probability, especially in scenarios with a large number of users.

A novel framework is introduced to integrate power allocation and scheduling for dynamic TDD systems by transforming them into graph theory problems. A dynamic TDD system operates by altering wireless communication protocols in real-time to optimize bandwidth usage. However, implementing this method introduces significant challenges related to power allocation and scheduling. A proposed approach transforms these challenges into graph theory problems by defining specific rules and objectives. Specifically, a dynamic TDD system is modeled as a series of discrete optimization problems, with each problem represented as a distinct graph theory problem. Two types of graphs are used: one for power allocation, represented as an edge-weighted graph with maximized total weight, and another for scheduling, represented as a graph with maximum total edge weight where no two adjacent edges have the same weight. A novel algorithm applies Monte Carlo methods to solve these graph theory problems. Monte Carlo methods involve randomly sampling possible solutions and selecting the best one. This algorithm works by randomly selecting different scheduling options and choosing the best one based on predefined criteria. A key feature of the proposed algorithm is its ability to handle large-scale TDD systems. The algorithm is evaluated on large-scale TDD systems and shows improved performance over existing algorithms.

Researchers have long been aware of the presence of topological defects known as vortices in superfluid $^4$He, and studies have shown that they can be quite mobile. A team of scientists has proposed the existence of a more basic defect within the superfluid, consisting of a single point defect that can move independently, and has been referred to as a monopole. Monopoles were initially hypothesized to have the same activation energy as vortices, but a new study has revealed a significant discrepancy in this energy for a specific interaction between the superfluid and a solid boundary. The researchers have also directly observed a monopole and its interaction with a vortex line by using a thin solid boundary to manipulate and study the defect. The findings of this study have shown that the activation energy for a monopole to cross a solid boundary in the presence of a nearby vortex line is over ten times greater than the same energy in the absence of a nearby vortex line, resulting in the monopole instead becoming pinned to the boundary when attempting to cross. The occurrence of this interaction has a very short timescale of roughly one nanosecond. The study has also demonstrated that the motion of a monopole is highly random and dispersed when not influenced by a solid boundary, with the ability to move several micrometers in a short period of time. The activation energy for this dispersed movement is found to be in the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-8}$

Researchers have a deep interest in the Ising model on a Cayley tree due to its connections with many systems and models. To investigate the effects of a uniform external magnetic field on the Ising model, particularly at its critical temperature, we have calculated the normalized cumulants of n spin values up to the 4th order.
