A cloud service, known as Cloud Error Recovery Cloud, was designed to identify and rectify performance deviations, ensuring seamless viewing. A cloud-based virtualization technique, known as Cloud Live Migration, was created to enhance system efficiency by transferring underperforming cloud servers to more advanced alternatives. A cloud-based quality assessment tool, known as Cloud Quality Analyzer, was developed to analyze performance metrics and streaming quality. A cloud-based security framework, known as Cloud Security Framework, was devised to safeguard against cyber threats. A cloud-based QoS management model, known as Cloud Cloud, was proposed to manage performance through cloud migration and quality assessment. A cloud-based architecture, known as Cloud Cloud, was designed to provide a scalable and efficient streaming system. A cloud-based experimental setup, known as Cloud Cloud, was established to test the system, utilizing Amazon EC2 and resulting in a 99.99% QoS level. A cloud-based future, known as Cloud Cloud, was proposed to enhance the system through advancements in cloud technology.

We've developed an analytical expression for the specific heat of doped graphene sheets, both with and without disorder, using the 2-SDRM renormalization approach. By incorporating the renormalized quasiparticle velocity and scattering time into a general carrier distribution function, we can determine the specific heat contribution. In the case of long scattering times, our model shows that the renormalized quasiparticle velocity follows a power-law behavior, which results in a linear temperature dependence of the specific heat in doped graphene, consistent with experimental findings.

In order to create more realistic and varied speech, we suggest utilizing co-occurrent speech data.  By leveraging this information, we show that speech synthesis models can produce higher quality speech naturally.  To support our claims, we introduce a novel method called MaskedSpeech, which builds on the Masked Autoregressive Neural Network framework.  This method involves masking speech segments to encourage the model to generate additional segments, resulting in a 20% reduction in perceived syntheticity and a 10% increase in naturalness when compared to the MNIST-style model.  When tested with external datasets, MaskedSpeech achieved a 5% increase in naturalness and a 4% decrease in syntheticity, outperforming the baseline model.  Additionally, we found that using additional segments improves performance even with limited data, resulting in a significant improvement of 14% in naturalness.  This suggests that MaskedSpeech is a robust and efficient method for generating more realistic and varied speech.

In one-dimensional nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations with harmonic and anharmonic potentials, we investigate the dynamics of solitary waves for both bounded and infinite domains. Our main findings include the following: (1) For the Klein-Gordon equation in an infinite domain, anharmonic forces can induce orbital instability for sufficiently large anharmonic coefficients. (2) In finite domains, we demonstrate that anharmonic forces always lead to orbital stability in both the Klein-Gordon and nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations. (3) In bounded domains, we obtain an explicit threshold value for the anharmonic coefficient that distinguishes between stability and instability in the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation. (4) In infinite domains, we identify the condition under which anharmonic forces induce instability in the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation.

Q-ball studies in theories with multiple stabilising symmetries are relatively unexplored.
This study delves into such theories, focusing on the scenario where the symmetries are related
as $U(1)_Y \times U(1)_X \times U(1)_A$, a pattern commonly found in grand unified theories.
It is demonstrated that the symmetries $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_X$ can combine to form a single $U(1)$
symmetry, leaving $U(1)_A$ as an independent symmetry.
Subsequently, Q-ball charge carriers are examined, determining the conditions under which the combined
$U(1)_Y \times U(1)_X$ symmetry results in negative contributions to the Q-ball energy, thus making
$U(1)_A$ the dominant stabilising symmetry.
Additionally, it is shown that the energy associated with the combined symmetry results in a minimum
when the charges of the scalar fields are in a specific ratio, providing further evidence that the
$U(1)_A$ symmetry is preferred when this ratio is violated.
Lastly, the study calculates the boson star energy for the $U(1)_A$ symmetry, revealing that it is
directly proportional to the vacuum energy when the symmetry charge is zero, a result that is
consistent with previous findings.

We have developed a novel model of cyclic universe cosmology that avoids the problem of future singularities for the holographic dark energy, utilizing the Granda-Oliveros approach. By introducing an adiabatic expansion phase and a specific cutoff method based on the difference between future and past singularities, we have determined that the de Sitter stage can be reached asymptotically. The proposed model demonstrates consistency with the calculations of the cyclic universe multiverse, as well as the periodic occurrence of the Big Rip singularity.

Given a graph G and a positive integer h that divides |G|, there exists a regular h-deged graph C that is a covering of G. The h-deged graph C is unique up to isomorphism and has a well-defined L-function, which is also an L-function of G. This relationship allows us to generalize some known graph L-function properties to their equivalents in h-deged graphs. Specifically, we prove that non-trivial irreducible representations of a group G can be used to construct an irreducible graph L-function F if and only if G has an odd prime factor, and we also determine the conditions under which a graph has a non-trivial irreducible graph L-function when its group has a prime factor of 2. Furthermore, we show that many graphs, including those with an abelian group, have a non-trivial irreducible graph L-function when their covering graphs have a specific property, and we provide examples of graphs with an abelian group that do not meet this criterion.

Let K be a finite non-abelian extension of the rational numbers Q, extended p times, with p being a prime, and assume the Galois group G of K is isomorphic to a free group on r generators for some integer r greater than 1. Let O_K denote the ring of integers of K and A_K its p-adic twist, obtained by setting A_K equal to O_K when p is 2. Given a non-trivial element g of G and a non-zero element x in K, we define phi as the associated Hom_G(g, G) map, extended to A_K for convenience, and then consider its associated ideal I in the ring A_K, on which G and phi exert a combined action. Under certain conditions, we establish that I is isomorphic to a non-trivial, freely generated right ideal in the ring I^e phi^e, with e representing the Galois group G acting cyclically, and this result holds for all sufficiently large p. If K is a finite non-abelian extension of the rational numbers Q, extended p times, with p being a prime, and the Galois group G of K is isomorphic to the alternating group S_3, we demonstrate that there exist infinitely many choices for the ideal I, and this result extends to certain solvable group configurations as well.

Researchers investigated the production of a long-lived neutral particle at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) using 13 TeV $pp$ collision data equivalent to 2.0 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The study focused on top-quark pair events with displaced decay signals, where the decay length of the long-lived particle-lifetime range- was probed across four distinct intervals: 3-10 mm, 10-30 mm, 30-60 mm, and 60-100 mm. To analyze these events, a data-driven background suppression technique was utilized, leveraging the characteristics of secondary vertices. The research employed a multivariate discriminant method to evaluate the sensitivity and estimate an upper limit on the long-lived particle's cross-section for each decay length interval, finding no significant findings and setting an upper limit of 1.18 pb (3.01 pb) for a 95% confidence level (95% exponential decay) across all decay length intervals.

Contextual models like BERT generate varying results when applied to the same word with different context, yet these differences are not solely due to how the model uses existing knowledge. It has been shown that some discrepancies arise purely from how the model handles probability rather than its semantic understanding. This work challenges the widely-held assumption that the semantic meaning of words changes over time by presenting counterarguments and supporting evidence from linguistic theories. As a result, we propose a new method to analyze the effects of context on word meanings by separating the impact of probability and semantic content. This approach is applied to analyze the semantic changes of words using the GLUE benchmark, and the findings suggest that the effects of probability are the primary drivers of contextual word meanings.

For ultra-light particles with a frequency-dependent mass influenced by a non-abelian symmetry at the microsymmetry scale, we make theoretical predictions that their mass is directly proportional to their Compton length, specifically $m_\phi = (m_{\rm Pl}^2 c^4/G_\phi)/(4\pi L_\phi^2)$. This relationship results in a mass as low as $10^{-22}$ eV for a given non-abelian group, making it possible for these particles to explain dark matter composition. Ultra-light particles can also take the form of vector, fermion, or scalar types, and when coupled to an inflaton, they could explain the 500 kHz anomaly in CMB B-modes. Furthermore, we suggest that ultra-light particles may be detectable through modified black hole spectroscopy or by analyzing the spectral lines of dark matter in the early universe.

To comprehend retinal development, it is crucial to understand how cell nuclei position themselves within the retina. Previous research suggested a random distribution of nuclei, but this study refutes that finding and instead reveals a distinct, non-uniform distribution of nuclei across the retina through retinal development. By analyzing video recordings of retinal cell migration, the authors demonstrate that the initial random movement of nuclei eventually becomes confined to specific areas, resulting in a non-uniform distribution. Additionally, by simulating retinal development using these findings, the authors show that the resulting distribution of nuclei can match those observed in actual retinas. This study provides the first direct evidence of dynamic retinal cell migration and a non-uniform distribution of nuclei, and it challenges the prevailing view of retinal development as a static process.

Compressive sensing, an efficient image acquisition technique, can be flawed if its matrix is poorly constructed. Research has shown that detrimental side effects result from high mutual coherence, even if exact recovery is still possible. A common approach to mitigate this issue is compressive sensing reconstruction with additional sparse constraints, but it comes with a heavy computational cost. In contrast, straightforward $l_1$ minimization yields superior results if the sensing matrix is modified to reduce mutual coherence. We introduce an efficient algorithm to decrease mutual coherence, making compressive sensing more practical for real-world applications. The method involves dividing the matrix into smaller blocks and rearranging their order to minimize coherence, and we provide an analytical expression for coherence in sparse circular Toeplitz matrices. The proposed technique outperforms existing solutions in terms of accuracy and computational time. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments, showing that it achieves precise image reconstruction. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub.

Active systems at equilibrium follow a scaled linearized hydrodynamics model, but this scaling breaks down in dimensions between 5 and 2, requiring a 6th dimension to fully capture dynamics without a stable linearized hydrodynamics. In this research, we demonstrate that active systems in dimensions between 5 and 2 exhibit an alternative scaling, which can be represented by a novel linearized hydrodynamics theory, even without a stable linearized dynamics. This discovery is confirmed through numerical simulations and analytical calculations of activity in linearized hydrodynamics in dimensions 3 and 2, which show an intriguing relationship with Apollonian packings.

Researchers and academics frequently rely on encrypted email services provided by public institutions, which often use the same security protocols as commercial services. Although these services are generally secure, a breach in their email communications could enable hackers to gain access to sensitive information. In order to mitigate this risk, it's essential to ensure the confidentiality of research data being transmitted over email. This paper introduces an innovative approach that leverages homomorphic encryption to enable secure multi-party collaborations. It allows multiple users to collaborate with large datasets while maintaining data confidentiality. In this system, users can not only collaborate with each other but also work with previously generated results. This is achieved through the use of a server that supports multiple users and enables homomorphic operations across all collaborating parties. This approach has several benefits, including the ability to perform complex operations on massive datasets and providing a scalable solution for research collaborations.

In cuprates, a Lifshitz transition within the normal state of optimally doped (Bi, Pb)$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_3$Cu$_4$O_{16+\delta}$ was discovered through thermal conductivity and optical conductivity measurements. This transition, located at ~160 K, is linked to an unusual vanishing point in the electron density of states, resulting from an exceptional vanishing point in the Fermi surface topology. The exceptional van Hove singularity, responsible for the Lifshitz transition, exerts a notable influence on the thermal conductivity via the electron-phonon interaction, leading to a notable thermal conductivity anomaly in the electron-dominant regime below the transition temperature.

To investigate the high-energy neutrino spectrum, detecting ultra-high energy cosmic neutrinos requires highly efficient neutron detection methods. A major challenge lies in distinguishing neutrons from gamma-rays, as the latter can mask neutrino observations. To mitigate this, we developed a novel technique for identifying neutrons using a Gadolinium-doped liquid scintillator. Gadolinium's high neutron capture cross-section and distinctive gamma-ray decay pattern enable precise detection of neutrons. In a test setup, we measured the neutron detection efficiency of this scintillator and validated our results through comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations. By incorporating Gadolinium, we observed a significant increase in detection efficiency, exceeding 99%. This advancement holds significant potential for improving the sensitivity of future large-scale neutrino detectors.

This research paper explores the existence of minimum problems that adhere to a certain condition, which can be expressed as a constraint involving a set that has a specific property. To this end, we first establish an alternative formulation of this constraint using another set with a different property, and then leverage that formulation to prove the existence of an optimal solution within the context of a specific functional space. Ultimately, this allows us to demonstrate the validity of the original problem under certain circumstances.

A recent study involving N-body simulations sought to explore the variety of planetary configurations that emerge in a vast sample of stellar systems. Focusing on small groups of stars with minimal interactions, the research examined how the properties of these systems affect the diversity of their planetary architectures. The findings show that a broad spectrum of complex planetary systems can develop through natural processes of stellar evolution and gravitational interactions. Ultimately, the results indicate that the range of planetary systems is significantly more extensive than its known instances.

The rapid growth of data requires the assistance of automated methods for initial text characterization, where NLP tools can aid in text extraction and normalization from unstructured documents containing IDs, licenses, and other official papers. Despite the progress made in NLP, a comprehensive set of tools specifically designed for this purpose is still lacking. Our research introduces IDFraser, a suite of 12 robust NLP tools that can characterize and normalize the content of ID-related documents, developed to enhance the quality of data harvesting. IDFraser is an open-source library, offering a comprehensive range of features, including tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, relationship inference, and text normalization, and is available under the permissive Apache-2.0 license.

The interplay between quantum coherence and classical simplicity in driven systems has generated significant interest in complex dynamics. A key aspect in this context is the behavior of coherent states within these systems. By examining su(1,1) systems under external driving forces, our research reveals that the damped motion of superposed states, when represented in phase space, forms closed trajectories. Our findings also show that the energy of these states follows periodic changes when driven by a harmonic force, and our analysis demonstrates the applicability of our approach to other types of driving forces. Notably, our results demonstrate that the coherent states' behavior can be described using a classical-like equation of state, and our study provides a fundamental framework for exploring the interplay between quantum coherence and classical simplicity in systems driven by external forces.

Our team conducted a comprehensive analysis of historical astronomical data using the Draper Interferometer at the University of Michigan, which revealed the presence of two previously unknown asteroids within the asteroid belt. Notably, one of these detected objects, designated as (10) Chios, showed rotational acceleration, which was confirmed through a re-examination of past observations. To determine the shape and composition of this asteroid, we performed a series of thermal and non-thermal force calculations based on its rotation, gravity, and interaction with the Sun's radiation. Our models suggested that (10) Chios has an irregular three-dimensional form and is composed of a mixture of carbon and silicate materials, which provides significant internal heat due to its slow rotation rate. Furthermore, we ran these simulations on a second discovered asteroid, (16) Psyche, which revealed that its shape could remain stable under gravitational forces from nearby asteroids.

Online discussions about politics are constantly changing, with users constantly joining and leaving communities of learners. Despite this constant evolution, communities of learners manage to maintain a strong sense of identity and coherence. To understand this coherence, we set out to analyze the factors that influence users to join new communities of learners or leave existing ones. By examining activity trails and community affiliations across multiple discussions, we identified key factors that encourage users to switch communities and also contribute to the development of community features over time. These factors, which include the appeal of a community, the distance between users and the influence of community leaders, ultimately shape the online political discussions and help identify potential figures of authority within these discussions.

Let $\Gamma$ be a subgroup of isometries on the interior of a compact surface $S$ that acts transitively and whose action is locally transitive on the surface's interior. We can determine whether $\Gamma$ is finitely generated based on a single surface parameter, $K$, which depends on the surface and its action, and satisfies specific bounds given the surface's topology. If the surface is of negative curvature and the action is locally transitive, we can determine whether $\Gamma$ is finitely generated based on a surface parameter $K_1$, which also depends on the surface and its action, and has a defined bound given the surface's topology. If the surface has a negative curvature and the action is locally transitive, we can determine whether $\Gamma$ is finitely generated based on a surface parameter $K_2$, which also depends on the surface and its action, and has a defined bound given the surface's topology and a specific topological condition.

A significant step has been taken in understanding M-dwarfs, thanks to an extensive analysis of nearly 300,000 exoplanet host stars. By examining the relationship between mass and the volume of M-dwarfs, researchers have refined this relationship and incorporated it into a user-friendly tool. This updated relationship can be utilized to determine the mass of low-mass stars encountered in exoplanet studies. By leveraging existing measurements of a star's volume and surface area, the new tool allows users to calculate the star's mass. This approach was validated through analysis of the M-dwarf sample used in the study. The researchers also explored potential applications of this relationship in future research and data analysis. Specifically, they discussed its potential use in identifying M-dwarfs that have been incorrectly classified as more massive stars. The new mass-radius relation is a valuable resource for researchers studying exoplanets and their host stars.

Graphene patches are used in the microdisk resonators to direct line waves in the optical field and thus shift their vibrational modes. The design of these graphene patches plays a significant role in line wave propagation and can lead to line waves transitioning to the optical domain. A theoretical analysis has been conducted to study line wave propagation and phonon exchange at the graphene interface. It was found that large graphene patches lead to line waves transitioning to the optical domain due to their thickness and proximity to the microdisk. Furthermore, a significant increase in phonon exchange occurs with larger graphene patches, resulting in a greater line wave frequency shift. Line waves can be switched on and off by adjusting the size of these graphene patches. A large frequency shift in line waves can be achieved by using larger graphene patches, which can be as thick as 100 nm.

Cheng and Korn have previously demonstrated that evaluating complex queries involving self-joins across multiple relations is only feasible in specific cases, even with the aid of materialized intermediate results. Building upon their work, they have developed a theoretical framework that defines and characterizes practical instances of such queries. Within this framework, they have created a set of formal criteria to determine when queries are considered 'tractable', and have shown that these criteria are both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, they have established that the evaluation of tractable queries can be broken down into more manageable sub-problems, allowing it to be efficiently solved via dynamic programming.

Determining whether a given set of polynomials corresponds to rational functions in a specific form is a fundamental problem in mathematics and computer science. When expressed in projective space, this problem becomes deciding if there are rational functions that map one projective variety to another to a specific variety, essentially checking if two varieties are "rationally isomorphic." Despite its importance, this problem has proven difficult to solve efficiently, even for simple cases like projective space. In a breakthrough study, it has been demonstrated that determining rational isomorphism requires significantly more computational power than previously thought, necessitating at least the same level of complexity as deciding whether a random number is even or odd.

The LHCb collaboration has measured the longitudinal polarization fraction P_long for B^0 decays to K^*0 K^0, and the difference in longitudinal polarization fractions, ΔP_long = P_long(B^0) - P_long(B_s^0), for B^0 and B_s^0 decays to K^+ K^- K^0, where K^*0 decays to K_S K^0 are not considered. The analyses utilize a combined 3 fb^-1 dataset collected by LHCb in 2010-2012. The measured values are P_long(B^0) = 0.378 ± 0.040 ± 0.011 and ΔP_long = 0.025 ± 0.040 ± 0.010, providing the first direct measurement of the distinct behavior of B^0 and B_s^0 systems in a CP-violating flavor system.

Reservoir computing is a cutting-edge method for complex system analysis, effectively handling systems with diverse time scales and multiple dynamic states, including those that are chaotic, oscillatory, or stuck in a steady state. However, understanding the underlying principles behind this success requires a deeper insight into the system's dynamics and the learning process. Using a delay-coupled linear system as an example, this study uncovers the underlying mechanisms behind reservoir computing through systems dynamics and learning by comparing its results with an analytical approach based on the theory of random processes. This comparison reveals that the system's temporal behavior is transformed into a set of independent signals by the reservoir, allowing for an independent learning of each signal by the readout layer. This learning results in a weighted combination of the signals that optimizes performance, and when mapped back to the original time domain, produces a time-dependent weight that reflects the system's dynamics. This weight can be adjusted to target specific dynamic states. This study demonstrates the practical applications of this approach by successfully learning and controlling multiple co-existing states in a chaotic system and a system with a homeostatic filter.

We introduce a novel estimator for the variance of a bias-reduced average treatment effect estimator, which is derived from a specific bias reduction method first introduced by Fruehwald and Sato (2020). We develop this estimator by applying a smoothing technique to a specific bias reduction method, and we demonstrate through simulations that our proposed estimator is an effective tool for controlling the standard error of the bias-reduced estimator. We also examine the theoretical properties of our proposed estimator, including its asymptotic distribution and bias properties.

We investigated how feedback control can be used to estimate the possible state combinations of a dynamic system within a given time frame. By leveraging discrete-time dynamic models and a state transition matrix, we developed an algorithm to calculate a states space matrix that predicts all potential states over any number of time steps. To refine this prediction and remove unnecessary possibilities, we applied a method to determine a maximum number of time steps in advance when the current state can be exactly replicated. This enables us to establish an upper limit for the number of states that need to be considered for any future time step, significantly reducing the complexity of the analysis. By using this approach in conjunction with an efficient numerical method, we demonstrated the ability to compute and visualize a large number of states over a large number of time steps.

Our research introduces an innovative approach to representing signals in high-dimensional spaces by utilizing local functionals, which builds upon established methods like Gaussian processes and support vector machines. By incorporating a novel decomposition technique, we successfully generalize previous work to achieve significant improvements in predicting high-dimensional signals. Notably, our method exhibits superior performance even with limited data, delivering highly accurate results for low-dimensional data and reasonable outcomes for higher dimensions. We have validated our approach through satisfying results on three challenging datasets, showcasing its potential to revolutionize the analysis of high-dimensional data dynamics.

Previous studies attempting to classify living things into categories have focused either on recognizing individual objects or analyzing groups of objects within a visual context. Conversely, research into perceiving animacy, a continuous and multifaceted property, has been overlooked. We propose that the animacy continuum should be viewed as a continuous spectrum of characteristics rather than a binary distinction between living and non-living things. We present a theoretical framework that models this continuum and incorporates visual categorizability and agency as two independent dimensions. We support this framework with three experiments, demonstrating that (1) visual categorizability and agency are distinct aspects of animacy, (2) objects' animacy is perceived based on their place on this continuous spectrum rather than a categorical classification, and (3) specific visual features contribute to animacy perception by indicating agency, self-mobility, and distinctness.

This study supplements our earlier research regarding the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros and confirms that a significant concentration of zeros on the critical line for all automorphic L-functions would imply the nonexistence of such zeros. Additionally, under certain conditions, we demonstrate that a substantial gap between the first and second zero lying on the critical line for all Hecke L-functions would lead to the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros.

This research develops a quantum relational Hoare logic, allowing us to formally verify the relationships between input and output values for programs in quantum computing, utilizing a relational Hoare logic framework originally proposed by Hoare in 1969.

To understand how super-spreader events impact infection rates within confined spaces, we developed an advanced model incorporating non-overlapping compartments for susceptible, infected individuals with varying contagiousness, and quarantined populations. Compared to traditional epidemiological models, our simulation showed that enclosed environment models predict significantly more infections from super-spreader events, resulting in a drastic increase in the basic reproduction number $R_t$ due to a small number of highly contagious individuals exponentially increasing infections among susceptible populations. Contrary to this, traditional models cap $R_t$ at the average number of infections per contagious individual, disregarding the impact of closed systems.

A $C_0$-semigroup of operators on a Banach space is considered codiskcyclic if its single-generated range covers the entire space codimension zero. This work delves into codiskcyclicity by examining operator semigroups, codiskcyclic vectors, and codiskcyclic subspaces within Banach space contexts. Specifically, key findings include: codiskcyclic vectors can be classified into the largest codiskcyclic subspace; this subspace coincides with the null space of the adjoint semigroup's codimension-one operator; and it also serves as the smallest codiskcyclic subspace. Conditions for codiskcyclic subspaces to align with the entire Banach space have been established, along with discussions on relevant applications and potential future inquiries.

Accurate information about a solar region's magnetic field is crucial for predicting the behavior of sunspots. This knowledge can be obtained through vector magnetic field maps, but these need to be regularly updated as the sun rotates. A key factor affecting the accuracy of these maps is the amount of magnetic field contributed by magnetic fields of both polarities within the same area. Researchers typically account for this by using a value called fill factor, which is the proportion of the area that is occupied by magnetic fields of one particular polarity. However, researchers have found that using this approach can sometimes lead to inaccurate results, especially when dealing with complex regions. As a result, they recommend using a different approach, called the magnetic fill fraction, which takes into consideration the strength of the magnetic field within a given area. By using this approach, researchers were able to create more accurate vector magnetic field maps, especially in complex regions, and found that the magnetic field is stronger than previously thought in about 30% of the area within the beta-beta region studied.

We analyzed a comprehensive dataset of young star clusters within nearby galaxies,
specifically the Large Magellanic Cloud, using a vast collection of 1.4 million pixels
across 104 square degrees from the Hubble/ACS. Our research reveals the density
evolution of these clusters by examining the surface density within distinct age
ranges. Initially, the density increases exponentially for clusters up to 50 million
years old, with a mean separation of 10 parsecs. However, for older clusters, the
density decreases logarithmically, reaching a mean separation of 100 parsecs. This
non-uniform density distribution affects the detection of clusters, with a higher
probability of finding younger clusters and influencing our view of the cluster
population. When accounting for field stars, our findings show a nearly uniform
cluster density across the bar and the outer wing regions. This research provides
new insights into the cluster population of the Large Magellanic Cloud and sheds
light on the past and present star cluster formation within this galaxy.

A new approach has been introduced for calculating the decay width of particles on a finite space, which takes into account the impact of bound states on the volume's mode density. This method has been specifically applied to the case of a complex scalar field decaying into two real scalar fields within a finite space, and a formula has been derived to calculate its decay width. The introduced approach takes into account how the finite space distorts the distribution of modes, and it results in an additional width component beyond what is predicted by the perturbation theory. The extra width component is directly calculable without needing to perform time-consuming simulations. It is also shown that it is possible to remove the edge effects by adding a small volume of empty space around the actual system, which would provide the same decay width readings. The introduced approach also enables the calculation of finite-space spectra, and it is demonstrated that the actual decay width can be obtained from the two-channel Bethe-Sommerfeld equations, which is in line with previous studies. The edge effects are further investigated by comparing the finite-space results with their infinite-space counterparts, and it is confirmed that the edge effects become less significant as the volume increases.

The Monte Carlo method is highly efficient when the target distribution is linear, in which case a simple affine transformation matches the distribution. Building on the success of affine transforms in computer graphics, we propose a novel layer called complex-valued affine coupling layer that significantly accelerates the sampling of complex-valued targets by using Monte Carlo methods, specifically for the residual network model used in image transformation tasks. In experiments, this layer consistently produces high-quality results and accelerates sampling times by a factor of 16 to 32, while only increasing computational overhead by a factor of 1.5, making it suitable for real-world applications that involve complex-valued targets and require fast sampling.

Under the Riemann Hypothesis, we derive an exact formula for the number of integers up to $x$ that are expressible as the sum of two square-free integers, with a specific asymptotic ratio that yields a value of $1$ as $x$ becomes very large. Additionally, our method allows us to determine the exact number of integers within the range $x$ to $2x$ that are the product of two square-free integers, with a resulting ratio of $\frac{2}{\log 2}\frac{\log x}{\log x} + o(1)$ as $x$ becomes very large. If the Riemann Hypothesis is true, we are able to accurately calculate the number of integers up to $x$ that are expressible as the product of three square-free integers, with a resulting ratio of $1$ as $x$ becomes very large.

The paper proves two key theorems regarding topological entropy in subshifts and shifts spaces. Firstly, it demonstrates that recognisable morphisms, when applied to any subshift, result in a subshift with the same topological entropy as the original subshift. Secondly, it shows that for any recognisable group, specifically when combined with periodic groups, the topological entropy is non-zero for certain shift spaces, and that this non-zero entropy is achievable through a recognisable morphism applied to a subshift with zero entropy.

Self-supervised pretraining of language models through masked language modeling has shown significant success, however, it's primarily limited to batch-wise optimization. This paper introduces the ReCross method, which takes self-supervised pretraining to a distributed level by leveraging the structural richness of parallel processed samples. By utilizing the latent representations learned from related parallel examples, the model can generate more accurate and diverse predictions for masked words. This leads to enhanced performance on multiple unsupervised evaluation tasks without the need for additional fine-tuning. Notably, the ReCross method outperforms the baseline model, even when reducing the amount of masked data, and achieves comparable performance to a model fine-tuned on the full dataset when evaluated on specific tasks.

This study introduces the m-ar-X (m-ar-K) function, a novel high-dimensional data reduction method based on the minimum spanning tree algorithm. By defining an intra-set distance as the maximum value among pairwise distances, the algorithm identifies the most compact subset of points that includes all data points, thus providing an alternative to traditional dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method equals or outperforms existing methods in terms of compression ratio while matching their accuracy.

The gaming industry faces evolving challenges in requirements engineering, 
notably requiring more effective methods to capture requirements' full scope, 
resolvable conflicts, and complete and up-to-date information. Although some 
requirements engineering approaches have been applied to this industry, there 
is a significant gap in research specifically focused on its needs. Our study 
utilizes a combination of existing research and a survey of the gaming industry, 
along with interviews and questionnaires, to explore the current practices, 
challenges, and requirements within the industry. Based on our findings, we 
identify several key areas for further research and propose a set of concepts, 
tools, and methods to address the requirements engineering challenges in the gaming industry.

Expensive computation and private data constraints make it difficult to optimize processes like hyperparameter tuning. Conventional methods like grid search aren't feasible due to the high cost of multiple runs. A new technique, private parallel random search, addresses this challenge by reducing the number of expensive computations required while protecting sensitive information.

In this study, we examine a particular configuration known as the double delta convention within the context of Coxeter groups. A specific arrangement, comprising multiple spheres within a wedge-shaped structure, has been identified, where each sphere corresponds to an edge of the Coxeter graph. A significant finding indicates that the number of these spheres is equivalent to the size of the minimal generating set for the Coxeter group. Moreover, the structure can be further analyzed to determine the group's presentation, resulting in a simplified form that reflects the relationships between the spheres and the graph's edges. This knowledge can be applied to determine the fundamental group of the arrangement, as well as the homeomorphisms between arrangements sharing the same graph, and providing a connection to the Kleinian group theory.

When analyzing astronomical data that involve correlated noise, using the standard method of calculating the chi-squared statistic can lead to inaccurate flux measurements due to over-smoothing. This paper presents an alternative approach that maintains the level of detail needed to account for noise structure at different spatial scales, thereby producing more precise flux estimates while still considering the effects of correlated noise. This new method can be applied in conjunction with traditional analyses that assume uncorrelated noise, and it is particularly effective when there is strong line emission on top of a background of varying noise characteristics.

The study of residual abundances in field blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars has provided valuable insights into the metallicity and the stellar mass of the Galactic bulge. However, the number of known BHB stars with detailed spectroscopic analyses is limited, hindering a more precise determination of the Galactic bulge's metallicity distribution. Using the large sample of BHB stars from the SPHERICAL GALAXY SURVEY, we perform an analysis of the metallicity distribution within the Galactic bulge based on the properties of BHB stars. By accounting for the effects of stellar mass and chemistry on the BBH sequence, we derive the metallicity distribution of the Galactic bulge for the -2 < [Fe/H] < 0.5 range. The resulting distribution shows a prominent metal-rich peak at [Fe/H] of -0.4, consistent with previous findings, and a less certain secondary component at more metal-poor values. The model also indicates a slight increase in the fraction of extremely metal-poor stars at [Fe/H] below -1.5.

We introduce a data-driven model that uses features and location information from social media to forecast the spread of rumors over time and their peak intensity. Unlike traditional models relying on complex mathematical assumptions, our approach leverages historical data to identify patterns and learns the attenuation effects of distance. We evaluate our method with real-world data from Weibo and find that it accurately predicts peak intensity and reduction with distance, outperforming basic forecasting techniques.

Using data on 1046 Fornax cluster planetary nebulae, we calculate the cluster's distance as approximately 19.3 kiloparsecs. Additionally, we determine the cluster's total luminosity function and radial distribution parameters. By comparing the Fornax cluster's planetary nebulae luminosity function to a similar function derived from 576 Centaurus cluster planetary nebulae, we find their distances to be 18.7 kiloparsecs and 15.6 kiloparsecs respectively. These findings support the previous observation of the Fornax cluster's mass concentration and the Centaurus cluster's mass deficit.

We introduce a groundbreaking new library called LifeStream, a cutting-edge set of high-performance algorithms designed to optimize the processing of large datasets that incorporate a wide range of numerical data types, including integers, floating-point numbers, and compact vector representations of real numbers. Unlike conventional processing methods that focus on either individual data points or entire dataset aggregates, LifeStream's innovative approach enables the flexible grouping of data by various criteria. In contrast to hand-optimized numerical libraries, LifeStream's performance is remarkably fast, with speeds rivaling top-tier numerical libraries even when working with extensive real-world datasets. Notably, LifeStream's exceptional performance is achieved without the need for intricate, hard-to-maintain low-level optimizations. Furthermore, LifeStream's code is remarkably transparent and easy to understand, with a simple and intuitive design that makes it a great fit for a wide range of scientific applications, including those involving data analysis, numerical computations, and compact vector representations.
This study defines Bertrand surfaces in 3-dimensional space and identifies specific surfaces in Euclidean space, hyperbolic space, and spherical space that serve as examples of Bertrand surfaces.

Under-represented loss functions like the KL Divergence often go unoptimized due to a lack of tailored optimization techniques. As a result, less common losses like KL Divergence are often approximated with more familiar options like the Mean Squared Error. This work challenges the assumption that certain advanced loss functions are impractical for use in neural networks. We investigate the impact of using less common losses in training networks and find that under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence can result in improved performance compared to more commonly used options like MSE. To facilitate the use of less common losses, we introduce a simple yet efficient optimization technique called Fixed Noise for neural network training. In fixed noise training, the optimization process is viewed as finding a single optimal input vector that minimizes the chosen loss function. This allows us to utilize loss functions that are difficult to differentiate, such as the KL Divergence, by treating the network's output as a fixed quantity. Experimental results show that our approach yields superior performance when using loss functions like the KL Divergence, outperforming traditional optimization methods and approximating MSE. FNT can be used in conjunction with batch normalization, and we find that combining FNT with BN results in even better performance.

This research investigates how an oblique feedback boundary condition affects the stability of the Navier-Stokes equations in a three-dimensional domain with a bounded area when the boundary is not aligned with the direction of mean flow. We initially establish the uniqueness of smooth solutions under this new condition. Next, we leverage damped tangent linear equations to obtain stability results for both periodic and non-periodic solutions. Finally, we verify that this oblique boundary feedback condition replicates the same effect as an oblique non-normal boundary condition, which we previously showed can lead to instability in certain situations.

The paper proposes a unified theory to capture the thermomechanical properties of polymers that undergo crystallization when stretched. It's interesting to note that previous models often relied on assumptions based on specific experimental observations, in contrast, this new approach grounds its predictions in fundamental thermodynamic and mechanical principles. The model includes a special treatment for the crystalline regions, where it applies the theory of finite strain elasticity, while for the amorphous regions it uses Flory-Huggins-like statistics to account for molecular interactions. The model also considers the effects of temperature and molecular weight on molecular configurations. The authors solve these coupled nonlinear differential equations numerically and verify that the solutions match the predicted behaviors of various polymers under different conditions, including changes in temperature, molecular weight, and applied stress. The model is also used to analyze the effects of molecular weight on the stress-strain curves of polymers and the resulting phase separation during stretching. The findings from this model are comparable to those obtained from other models and experimental results.

A comprehensive theory to understand the topological characteristics of a Fermi surface's magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials has been developed, accounting for any shape deformation caused by superconductivity. This theory reveals that the susceptibility is determined by the surface's topological features rather than its local characteristics, and can be calculated using a novel formula based on the surface's topological index. The practical application of this theory is demonstrated through the calculation of susceptibility for several materials, including copper oxides, graphite, and iron-based superconductors, and how it relates to their superconducting properties.

In diverse real-world scenarios, a model can learn from feedback provided by a teacher who aims to correct errors made during a task. However, the effectiveness of this feedback relies on the assumption that the teacher's intention is to guide the model towards the correct task outcome. We introduce an innovative approach, influenced by game theory, to determine whether the teacher's feedback is indeed intended for the model's benefit. This approach involves assessing the degree to which the teacher's actions are motivated by a desire to aid the model, relative to the space of all possible actions. We call this the "value" of the teacher's action. We show that by utilizing this value function, we can determine whether the teacher is providing helpful feedback that aligns with the model's goals. Furthermore, this value function enables us to distinguish the teacher's helpful feedback from other actions that the model may mistakenly interpret as guidance. We demonstrate the benefits of using the value function in several scenarios, including multi-agent settings and systems with various types of noise and diversity.

Conventional differential detection is enhanced through the use of assisted information at the receiver, specifically for continuous phase modulation signals. By comparing conventional and assisted differential detection, it is found that the assisted method offers a significant improvement of approximately 6 dB in error rate for CPM. The assisted technique is shown to be an optimal detector for CPM with a differential delay of one symbol, achieving the same performance as coherent detection while maintaining the simplicity of differential detection.

Researchers utilized the Large Neutron Star Compact Object Storage Grid (LNS) that contains over 300,000 neutron-star radius measurements to examine the distribution of this parameter. They discovered a slight bias towards smaller radii when considering only published values, but found no significant evidence of a specific range. By analyzing the source of potential biases within the LNS, a notable gap in measurements below 10 kilometers was identified. It was also found that smaller radii are more likely to be selected for publication, and that the distribution of authors exhibits a preference for smaller radii. The radius distribution is crucial for predicting the likelihood of an electromagnetic counterpart during black-hole and neutron-star mergers, and understanding the potential biases within the LNS is essential for accurately utilizing this data in future observations with the Square Kilometre Array.

The paper discusses the applicability of the grand canonical ensemble when varying pressure in a system of interacting particles. It asserts that the grand canonical ensemble is only viable when the compressibility at a given pressure is sufficiently low. The argument is supported by a mathematical derivation, which indicates that the condition $e^{\beta p V N}$ is small is necessary for the grand canonical ensemble to be valid. The paper also provides an alternative, more direct criterion based on the fourth cumulant, which is also related to the compressibility at a given pressure. The discussion is illustrated with examples of hard spheres, Yukawa particles, and Stewarta-Mies cells. The paper concludes by suggesting that the compressibility at a given pressure serves as an essential control parameter in experiments involving the expansion of systems of interacting particles.

Images containing both rain streaks and removed regions pose a significant challenge for image restoration techniques. To overcome this challenge, research has focused on estimating multiple images, including the original image, rain streaks, and removed regions, by correlating these components. However, this approach has limitations due to the high dimensionality of the problem. In contrast, we propose a novel approach that views rain generation and removal as complementary operations, defined by invertible transformations, allowing us to model rain streaks and removed regions as a single, integrated process. By applying our method to this process, we can generate multiple images, including the original image, rain streaks, and removed regions, from a single input image, by running a backward pass, and vice versa. The key component of our method is a rain removal module, defined by an invertible transformation, that takes an image and produces rain streaks, and a synthesis module that combines the image and rain streaks to recreate the removed regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by conducting extensive experiments on a newly created dataset, named Rain12, which consists of 12,000 training images, 6,000 validation images, and 6,000 test images, and achieving superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques.

Human evaluators compare diverse items like products, advertisements, and microtask assignments, and their feedback is crucial for learning a rewarding function.
Despite the benefits of comparing multiple items at once and reducing the need for individual comparisons, current methods are limited to only considering basic comparison rules, such as comparing two items, or risk overestimating the value of items that are highly ranked in a batch.
We address these challenges by developing a new algorithm that learns from human feedback on batch comparisons of items, taking into account the uncertainty of its estimates and ability to handle an arbitrary comparison graph.
Our method learns a valuable function over items by maximizing the likelihood of its estimates, and we prove that it can distinguish between possible and impossible comparison graphs.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting the first publicly available evaluation of reward learning from batch comparisons, showing that it outperforms baseline methods that use individual comparisons or naive comparison rules, and provides a way to analyze the uncertainty of estimates based on human feedback alone.

In this research, we explore set theory axioms across various signatures, noting that no signature exists where set theory possesses a unique model companion. To demonstrate this, we present a multitude of signatures existing beyond those analyzed by Kayser in 'The Existence of Model Companions in Set Theory' for which set theory's model companions do not exclusively exist. Moreover, using a technique introduced by Tsadik in 'On the Existence of Model Companions for Finite Structures', we demonstrate the existence of countless signatures enabling set theory to possess a model companion.

In this research, we have been able to verify the existence of multiple solutions for a Branson-Paneitz type equation on R^n with specific types of boundary conditions, specifically including the Steklov type boundary condition, for 5<=n<=7.

Our analysis of European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction data from 2007 to 2019 revealed correlations in consumption patterns across various psychoactive substances, including heroin, cocaine, amphetamines, ecstasy, and new psychoactive substances. The study examined consumption trends in nine countries, identifying common fluctuations across the region and distinguishing local trends within these patterns. The data were analyzed using a combined approach of statistical methods and time-series plots to detect overall and country-specific trends. The results highlighted the importance of considering regional trends when analyzing local consumption data, as well as potential global trends among drug consumers.

Previous studies have demonstrated that neural models are capable of recognizing the underlying hierarchical structure of relations in if-then statements. Contrary to conventional wisdom that neural networks must be trained on complex tasks before exhibiting hierarchical organization in their internal representations, our findings suggest that models such as BERT are initially unaware of these relations. Our research indicates that models can acquire this understanding through training and testing on relation hierarchies in a task-agnostic manner. We further discover that models with this knowledge can perform well on complex tasks involving these relations, even in cases where the relation hierarchy is altered. Our results imply that neural models possess a degree of neural plasticity, allowing them to adapt hierarchical relations learned in a task-agnostic manner to accommodate new information.

Our research introduces NISQ-HHL, a modified version of the HHL algorithm, designed to be more efficient for near-term quantum computers. Although the HHL algorithm significantly reduces the required number of oracle calls and qubit operations compared to other quantum simulation methods, its application is hindered by the need for highly precise amplitude estimation. In contrast, NISQ-HHL allows for an acceptable loss of precision in exchange for a substantial decrease in needed oracle calls and qubit operations, making it suitable for simulation tasks involving large systems.

To effectively utilize large-scale pre-trained models for automated speech recognition, leveraging the strong multimodal connections in these models is crucial. By introducing the bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM), our work allows for the exploration of these connections. Specifically, BiAM establishes a direct connection between speech representations and the attention on linguistic information, thereby preventing the interference from other irrelevant attention. Through the enforcement of a constraint on the sum of attention probabilities, BiAM is further optimized to prioritize essential linguistic information. Our method, BiAM, is incorporated into the Transducer system, leading to notable improvements of 4.3% in word error rates (WER) on the Librispeech validation set and 3.2% on the test set.

In the 2D Euclidean space, certain specific stationary shapes have unique properties confirmed mathematically. To gain insight into these properties in higher-dimensional space, this research analyzes stationary shapes in 3D and 4D Euclidean space and uncovers related unique properties, confirming their connection to calibers in these higher-dimensional spaces.

Consider a one-lane road of finite length with entry and exit points, where n vehicles arrive at a Poisson process with rate n and follow independent routes. Let D_k^(n) denote the distribution of the kth parking space, where k is large enough that the distribution can be approximated as a continuous function. It has been proven that the total variation distance between D_k^(n) and its limiting distribution D_k, as well as the Kolmogorov distance, both converge to 0 at a rate of O(1/√n). Additionally, it has been shown that the moment method can be used to determine the moments of D_k, and that these moments correspond to solutions to a specific system of equations that can be solved through an iterative process. As a result, we are able to establish the convergence of the kth parking space distribution to a specific limit distribution D_k, and are also able to determine the moments of this limit distribution for any positive integer k.

Our research reveals that the critical voltage of superconducting nanowires can be precisely adjusted by an odd parity symmetry in the Josephson junction, which arises from the misalignment of the nanowire's spin-orbit fields. This odd parity symmetry causes a $\pi$ phase junction to behave like a zero-phase junction when the applied voltage is odd, and vice versa, when the applied voltage is even.

In 1995, the discovery of GJ 229B provided the first clear evidence of a brown dwarf associated with a stellar companion. Initially, researchers speculated that GJ 229B's formation was similar to that of a planet, given its small mass and the long period of its orbit around the G-type main sequence star GJ 229A. However, new observations made possible by the SPHERE instrument on the VLT have allowed us to study the properties of GJ 229B's atmosphere. Using these observations along with those from the ESO's X-Shooter, the Mauna Kea's CANOE, and the Keck Observatory's NIRSPEC, we analyzed the spectral data to determine the chemical composition of GJ 229B's atmosphere. Our analysis revealed a diverse range of elements, including carbon, oxygen, and iron, which show an abundance similar to that of the Sun. This finding, combined with the absence of absorption from certain elements in GJ 229B's atmosphere, suggests that it has an atmosphere that is interacting with its stellar companion. This interaction may be the result of a stellar wind or an outflow from the brown dwarf itself. As a result, the new data on GJ 229B's atmosphere contribute to our understanding of the complex processes involved in forming objects that fall between planets and stars.

A parton distribution function for a quark population within a quark-gluon plasma is determined, and its probability density, denoted as $f(x)$, is found to be directly proportional to $x$ within the temperature range $0.7T_c \leq T \leq 0.9T_c$, where $T_c$ is the critical temperature for the transition from a normal to a quark-gluon plasma state.

Recent advances in the study of video viewpoint awareness have incorporated recurrent models and synthetic training data. In contrast, we contend that videos can be analyzed through a single pass over the footage, using a single viewpoint, and that representation bias can be minimized through an opposing framework. Utilizing a single-pass model allows for real-time processing of videos. During training, a dual framework allows us to directly minimize the bias in our representation. We developed a novel single-pass model known as the single-frame-from-action network, in addition to a dual representation learning framework known as the synthetic-to-real contrastive framework. By utilizing a data representation that is independent of bias, we were able to enhance the accuracy of novel-viewpoint image generation from just a single-view video. Our results show that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques on the SUN3D dataset.

Highly sensitive phase measurements are crucial in applications such as interferometry and quantum computing. Conventionally, anodized waveguides are used to determine the phase of light based on changes in transmission, but they have limitations due to mode transitions and deflections. A novel method has been developed to build a precise phase beam splitter using a parabolic photonic waveguide that takes advantage of high-frequency mode combinations. Theoretical modeling and experimental validation show that this design can accurately measure phase shifts with high sensitivity, outperforming traditional anodized beam splitters. The proposed design also exhibits mode stability, eliminating the need for mode transition correction. A 10.6 um parabolic waveguide was used in the experiment, and the results demonstrate phase measurements with high precision, with a coefficient of variation of 0.0475 for ~pi phase shifts. The simplicity and high precision of this design make it suitable for high-sensitivity phase measurements in applications such as quantum computing and interferometry.

In quantum mechanics, the mass spectra of different baryon states correspond to specific energy levels within the baryon potential well, mirroring the energy levels of a hydrogen atom. Researchers have historically attempted to derive these levels through elementary constituent interactions, but their findings have not fully aligned with the observed data due to the complexity of interactions involved. However, studies have shown that interactions between quarks and the gluons responsible for them can be represented in a simpler form, allowing for the derivation of mass spectra through the Schr\"{o}dinger equation. In this work, we utilize this approach to calculate the mass spectra of a range of baryon states consisting of three quarks, utilizing the established potential well parameters. The results show an excellent agreement with the available data, further validating the quark-gluon interaction model and the Schr\"{o}dinger equation approach.

A model of aerosol dispersal, centered on the idea of well-mixed air, has been widely adopted but its accuracy has not been thoroughly assessed, particularly when subjected to realistic ventilation conditions. To address this, we've simulated the behavior of aerosols around an infected individual using both the well-mixed model and a more advanced approach that takes into account turbulent flows, for various ventilation settings and room dimensions. The results show significant discrepancies between the two models, with the well-mixed model overestimating aerosol concentrations by as much as 300 times. The discrepancy is greatest in rooms with poor ventilation and small sizes. The inaccuracy of the well-mixed model is so great that it may actually predict the wrong outcome, even if we consider the uncertainty in the number of aerosols produced by an infected individual. The issue is critical because it may impact the effectiveness of control measures, such as mask usage. To mitigate this inaccuracy, we've explored alternative approaches, such as using a simplified model that focuses on the average distance aerosols travel, and found that these models perform similarly to the more advanced approach. The inaccuracy of the well-mixed model highlights the need to carefully validate any model of aerosol behavior and to consider the potential risks of oversimplifying complex phenomena.

The phenomenon of quantum vacuum observing x-ray photons propagating through medium made up of electrons, specifically in helium gases, has been studied and a notable effect identified. Depending on the angle of propagation, an abrupt shift in the speed of propagation from greater than to less than the speed of light in a vacuum occurs. This phenomenon of varying speed is influenced by the direction of propagation and the presence of atomic resonances and is demonstrated using a combination of classical and quantum theories. A notable effect, quantum vacuum diffraction, is also observed, showing that even in the absence of interactions with atoms, an irregular pattern of transmission occurs due to the influence of electron pairs. The comparison of calculated data to actual measurements reveals a match, proving that these effects are genuine and require a quantum vacuum perspective to be understood.

We introduce an algorithm in 3D space that produces polyhedra with the ability to translate in any direction. Notably, this algorithm yields the same outcome as the method proposed by Berman in 2D space, which generates polyhedra that can translate in any direction. The algorithm we introduce also shares a connection with the construction of figure-eight shaped polyhedra and can also be adapted to create polyhedra with translational symmetry in 4D space.

Our research builds upon a 2010 conjecture of Goldwasser, Kalai, and Kilian regarding the relationship between unclonable encryption, copy-protection for unlearnable functions, and neural networks. We initially analyze the security of their proposed unclonable encryption scheme in the context of a dishonest user with a powerful neural network. We then investigate the implications of our findings for copy-protection and neural networks. Additionally, we explore connections to the learning with errors problem and the hybris problem from the literature.

A fundamental concept in coding theory is the idea of generating multiple messages from a single message by utilizing a code with a large rate. This concept is often employed in channel coding for error correction. In this research, we have developed a novel approach to create a variety of messages from a single original message by modifying an existing code with a high rate. This novel method is utilized in our paper to investigate methods of modifying pre-existing channel codes to achieve authentication codes. Specifically, we explored the possibility of producing an infinite number of distinct messages, each representing a different asymptotically negligible coding rate, from a single original message. We established an upper limit on the number of these distinct messages and defined a new parameter, gamma, which characterizes this limit and is at least as large as 1/2 in any legitimate coding scheme. Moreover, we demonstrated the feasibility of achieving any desired level of gamma greater than 1/2 by modifying specific types of codes, such as those with high rate and low error probability, and we provided a general approach to achieve any desired level of gamma greater than 1/2.

Using density functional theory and the GW method, we investigate how lattice structures and doping levels influence the energies and dispersion of plasmons in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$. Our analysis considers a range of lattice relaxations and doping concentrations for three specific twisting angles commonly studied, and compares the outcomes to experimental data. The findings highlight the significance of accurate lattice parameters and doping levels on plasmon behavior, and reveal that interlayer coupling, twisting angle, and doping level all impact the plasmon energy in distinct ways.

In this study, we examine almost conformal Ricci solitons on a complete oriented manifold of dimension four, establishing necessary and sufficient criteria for them to be almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons. Furthermore, we derive a condition for almost conformal Ricci solitons to be almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons in terms of the almost conformal potential function, provided that the conformal almost Ricci soliton is not a conformal gradient Ricci soliton.

The magnetospheres of stellar and planetary varieties share a common thread - they are both fueled by the interaction of plasma and magnetic fields. Yet, their sources and consequences differ remarkably. In stellar systems, magnetic fields are shaped by the stars' strong winds, whereas in planetary systems, plasma and magnetic interactions are rooted in the planets' internal fields. A notable parallel between the two lies in the similarity of their dynamic behavior, characterized by mass and size differences. Recent research has particularly focused on the impact of stellar winds on the magnetospheres of close-in planets and the potential for magnetic reconnection to influence the dissipation of angular momentum. Conversely, the influence of planetary plasma on their surrounding environments is only beginning to be explored. Further study of these relationships will be crucial in understanding the long-term stability of planetary magnetic connections and their host stars' rotation.

Researchers examined the electrical properties of Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers using direct current and alternating current measurements. By separating the Bismuth layers into thin and thick categories based on their average width, a distinct transition in behavior around 6 nanometers was observed. This transition is explained by a shift from a coherent scattering mechanism to an incoherent one. The coherent regime is influenced by magnetic Cobalt domains, while the incoherent regime is influenced by the random movement of electrons across the multilayer boundaries. This transition is further confirmed by time-difference measurements of the Hall effect, showing a coherent scattering time that decreases linearly with increasing Bismuth thickness below 6 nanometers, and an incoherent scattering time that remains relatively constant at approximately 0.13 picoseconds.

This study examines the ground state and dipole density distribution of a fractional $n$-dimensional Schrödinger equation with an inverted harmonic oscillator potential, as well as the behavior of its energy levels for $n=1$ and $n=2$. The ground state wave function and energy are expressed in terms of Gamma functions, and the analysis shows how they are affected by the fractional parameter $\alpha$, the inverted potential strength $k$, and the number of spatial dimensions $n$. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the exact relationship between the energy levels of the fractional and ordinary Schrödinger equations, and it finds that the former converges to the latter as $\alpha$ approaches 1.

Researchers initially assumed that the optimal regularization method for neural networks involves constraining their $p$-norm, where $p$ is a large number, due to a common assumption that large $p$-norms are more effective at limiting a network's Lipschitz constant. However, it has not been proven whether this assumption holds true. In fact, studies have shown that different neural networks perform differently in relation to their $p$-norm and Lipschitz constant. For instance, a fully connected neural network's performance is more closely tied to its 2-norm than its $p$-norm, whereas an average-activated neural network's performance is more closely tied to its 1-norm than its 2-norm. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that training an average-activated neural network with a bounded Lipschitz constant is equivalent to training a neural network with a bounded 1-norm using standard optimization methods.

Sequential models like LSTMs are widely used in analyzing sentence structures due to their ability to grasp long-range dependencies. Langer and Stede investigate how LSTMs rely on local information to recognize hierarchical relationships within sentences by running a series of experiments. They examine various tree configurations, sequence models, and evaluation methods to gain insights into LSTMs' performance based on sentence hierarchy. Findings suggest that LSTMs primarily use local heuristics to understand sentence structure, and also present a new approach to analyzing the accuracy of sequence models on hierarchical sentences. Langer and Stede's work provides a framework for evaluating sequence models' understanding of sentence structure and suggest that future models like transformers should be assessed for their ability to recognize hierarchical relationships within sentences.

HD80606b, a planet that passes in front of its host star, undergoes significant temperature fluctuations due to its close proximity. As it approaches the star, its surface temperature increases, and as it recedes, it cools down. Observations of this process, known as transit, can be used to study the planet's atmospheric properties. By analyzing data from multiple telescopes, a team of astronomers was able to study the planet's temperature changes and its effects on the surrounding material. HD80606b passes in front of its host star about every 43 days, and as it does so, a mini-eclipse, or transit, occurs. During this event, a small portion of the star's light is blocked, and the planet's atmosphere interacts with the surrounding material, causing a small drop in the star's brightness. By analyzing the data from these transits, astronomers were able to study the planet's atmospheric properties and the surrounding material, known as the circumstellar disk, and found that the planet's temperature rose to over 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 degrees Celsius) during the closest point in its orbit, known as periastron, and that the circumstellar disk was heated to about 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit (1,000 degrees Celsius).

Physical therapy exercises are often monotonous and unappealing, causing some patients to skip sessions. To enhance the rehabilitation process, gamification can make exercise routines enjoyable, balancing the therapeutic benefits with the pleasure of playing games. A crucial factor in this balance is the interaction design, particularly in experiences that engage patients through the gamified exercises themselves. We take the approach of integrating interaction parameters with balance goals to create a framework for co-design. This framework allows therapists and designers to collaborate in balancing rehabilitation and engagement by jointly considering the effects of interaction parameters on exercise outcomes and player experience. We applied this framework in a case study involving a gamified exercise for shoulder mobility, collaborating on its design to balance the rehabilitation of impaired deltoid muscles and the enjoyable experience of playing a virtual fishing game. The outcome of this collaboration was validated through usability tests and analysis of user data.

This study explores the relationship between geometrically nonlinear elasticity and its linearised counterpart, as well as their connection to brittle fracture energies within periodic minimal surfaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that geometrically nonlinear elasticity corresponds to a triple of measures comprising the surface tension and two additional terms related to the linearised elasticity, which in turn can be interpreted as the square of the surface tension when restricted to the same class of fractals. Conversely, linearised elasticity corresponds to the sum of surface tension and an additional term that can be seen as (a fractional) square of surface tension when considered within the same class of sets.

To enhance signal recognition in LHC searches for vector leptoquarks, we've developed a detailed description at next-to-leading order plus soft part, using in-house code that incorporates resummation techniques and threshold logarithm calculations, often incorporated into commercial programs like 

A novel deep-neural-network (DNN) model has been proposed to enhance low-dose PET images in conjunction with MRI data, and the effectiveness of using two different MRI protocols in the reconstruction process was investigated. To mitigate the adverse effects of low-dose PET scans, such as reduced image resolution and increased noise levels, a comprehensive study was conducted. Initially, a DNN model utilizing MRI data was explored to improve the quality of low-dose PET images. Notably, the results showed a notable improvement in the quantitative measurement of the standard uptake value (SUV) and the lesion detectability index (LDI) when using the proposed DNN model, with SUV and LDI values increasing by 5.3% and 12.5%, respectively. Furthermore, when using co-registered MRI data, the DNN model yielded comparable results to the deep-co-training (DCT) model. Interestingly, utilizing unregistered MRI data led to a 104% improvement in SUV and a 26.5% improvement in LDI when compared to the traditional iterative expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm.
